lessons.title: Ecosystems and Biogeochemical Cycles
lessons.notes_html:
Ecology is the study of the relationships between living organisms and their environment. The word ecology was coined by Ernst Haeckel. The term ecosystem was coined by Arthur George Tansley in 1935.

Biogeochemical Cycles

A biogeochemical cycle is the pathway through which elements (such as carbon, oxygen, nitrogen and water) circulate between living organisms and the non-living environment. Through these cycles the essential elements are used again and again by organisms.

The Oxygen Cycle

In the oxygen cycle, oxygen circulates between the atmosphere, living organisms and the earth. Plants release oxygen into the atmosphere during photosynthesis. Animals and plants use this oxygen for respiration and release carbon dioxide, which plants again use for photosynthesis. In this way the amount of oxygen in the atmosphere stays balanced.

Resources of an Ecosystem

  • Biotic resources — the living organisms: producers, consumers and decomposers.
  • Abiotic resources — the non-living components such as sunlight, air, water, soil, minerals and temperature, which organisms need to live and grow.

mcqs.why: All green plants carry out photosynthesis and release oxygen into the atmosphere; animals and plants then use this oxygen for respiration.

mcqs.why: Animals and plants use oxygen for respiration and release carbon dioxide, which plants again use for photosynthesis, so the amount of oxygen in the atmosphere stays balanced.

lessons.title: Food Chains, Food Webs and Energy Flow
lessons.notes_html:
The sun is the primary source of energy in an ecosystem. Green plants (producers) trap the energy of the sun and change it into chemical energy during photosynthesis.

Trophic Levels

Primary consumers eat the producers, secondary consumers eat the primary consumers, and so on — these feeding levels are called trophic levels. The feeding level of an organism in an ecosystem is called its trophic level. The amount of energy at each trophic level decreases as it moves through the ecosystem, because much energy is used in life activities and lost as heat. Decomposers like bacteria and fungi break down dead bodies and return nutrients to the ecosystem.

Food Chain and Food Web

  • A food chain is a single, straight pathway showing who eats whom, e.g. grass → grasshopper → frog → snake.
  • A food web is a network of many interconnected food chains — a highly integrated diagram that shows the food connections among different species in an ecosystem.

The graphical representation of the trophic relationship of organisms in an ecosystem is called an ecological pyramid.

mcqs.why: The sun is the primary source of energy in an ecosystem; green plants trap its energy and change it into chemical energy during photosynthesis.

mcqs.why: Green plants are the producers; they trap the energy of the sun as chemical energy in photosynthesis, and consumers then eat the producers.

mcqs.why: Decomposers like bacteria and fungi break down dead bodies of organisms and return the nutrients to the ecosystem.

lessons.title: Relationships Between Organisms: Symbiosis and Predation
lessons.notes_html:
Symbiosis is a relationship which occurs when organisms interact in a way that benefits one or both of them.

Types of Symbiosis

  • Mutualism — both species benefit, e.g. butterflies and flowers: butterflies get food from flowers and the flowers are pollinated.
  • Commensalism — one species benefits while the other is neither helped nor harmed, e.g. a small plant growing on the trunk of a big tree for support.
  • Parasitism — one organism (the parasite) benefits while the other (the host) is harmed, e.g. a tick on an animal.

Predation

Predation is a relationship between two organisms in which one organism (the predator) hunts, kills and eats the other organism (the prey). In predation one organism is benefited while the other is harmed. Consumers that actively hunt other organisms are called predators.

mcqs.why: Symbiosis occurs when organisms interact in a way that benefits one or both of them; its types are mutualism, commensalism and parasitism.

mcqs.why: In predation one organism is benefited (the predator, which gets food) while the other (the prey) is harmed, because it is killed and eaten.

mcqs.why: The small plant benefits by getting support, while the big tree is neither benefited nor harmed — the book gives this as the example of commensalism.

lessons.title: Global Warming, Pollution and Protecting the Environment
lessons.notes_html:
The unwanted and harmful change in the environment is called pollution. Most environmental problems are caused by human activities.

Global Warming

The main causes of global warming are: burning of fossil fuels in vehicles and industries, which releases large amounts of carbon dioxide; overpopulation; deforestation; and the release of other greenhouse and toxic gases into the atmosphere.

Global warming is harmful because it raises the temperature of the earth. It melts glaciers and ice caps, raises the sea level and causes floods, disturbs rainfall and climate, harms crops and destroys the habitats of many species, pushing them towards extinction.

Endangered Species

The species of living organisms which are decreasing day by day are called endangered species.

Improving the Environment

Humans can improve the environment by planting more trees, stopping deforestation, reducing the burning of fossil fuels, using vehicles less, controlling pollution from factories, protecting endangered species and keeping their surroundings clean.

lessons.title: The Neuron: Structure and Types
lessons.notes_html:
The study of the nervous system is called neurology. The neuron (nerve cell) is the structural and functional unit of the nervous system.

Parts of a Neuron

  • Dendrites — short, branched fibres which receive messages and carry them towards the cell body.
  • Cell body — contains the nucleus and cytoplasm and keeps the cell alive.
  • Axon — the long fibre which carries the nerve impulse away from the cell body to other neurons or to an effector; in many neurons it is covered by a fatty myelin sheath which speeds up the impulse.

Types of Neurons

  • Sensory neuron — carries messages from the receptors (sense organs) towards the brain and spinal cord.
  • Motor neuron — carries messages from the brain or spinal cord to the effectors (muscles and glands).
  • Inter-neuron — the neuron which decides about the action for a certain stimulus; it links sensory and motor neurons.

Receptors are the cells, tissues or organs that detect stimuli, e.g. the sense organs — eyes, ears, nose, tongue and skin. Effectors are the parts which respond to the messages of the nervous system: the muscles and glands of the body.

mcqs.why: The cell body contains the nucleus and cytoplasm and keeps the neuron alive; dendrites bring messages to it and the axon carries them away.

lessons.title: The Brain: Cerebrum and Its Hemispheres
lessons.notes_html:
The cerebrum is the largest part of the human brain. It is the centre of intelligence, memory, consciousness and thinking. It receives messages from the sense organs, interprets them and decides the responses; it controls all voluntary actions of the body.

Left and Right Hemispheres

The cerebrum is divided into left and right hemispheres.

  • The left hemisphere controls the right side of the body and handles logical thinking, language, writing and mathematical work.
  • The right hemisphere controls the left side of the body and handles creativity and emotional processing, art and music.

The most developed nervous system exists in humans.

lessons.title: Midbrain, Hypothalamus, Cerebellum and Spinal Cord
lessons.notes_html:
Midbrain

The midbrain is a small part of the brain present below the cerebrum; it connects the forebrain with the hindbrain and controls some movements of the eyes and ears (reflex movements of head, neck and trunk).

Hypothalamus

The hypothalamus controls body temperature, hunger, thirst and emotions, and links the nervous system with the hormonal (endocrine) system.

Cerebellum

The cerebellum is involved in precise and accurate body movements — it coordinates balance and posture.

Medulla Oblongata

The medulla oblongata controls involuntary actions such as the heartbeat and breathing.

Spinal Cord

The spinal cord is the most important structure between the body and the brain. It is a long, cylindrical cord of nervous tissue running inside the backbone (vertebral column). It carries messages between the brain and the rest of the body through spinal nerves, and it is also the centre of reflex actions.

lessons.title: Reflex Action, Reflex Arc and Brain Health
lessons.notes_html:
A reflex action is an immediate, involuntary and automatic response to a stimulus, e.g. pulling the hand away from a hot object.

The Reflex Arc

The path of the nerve impulse during a reflex action is called a reflex arc. Its pathway is:

Receptor → Sensory neuron → Inter-neuron (in the spinal cord) → Motor neuron → Effector

When a finger touches a hot object, the impulse travels from the receptor in the skin through the sensory neuron to the spinal cord, then through the motor neuron to the arm muscle (effector), and the hand is pulled away at once.

Voluntary and Involuntary Actions

  • Voluntary actions — under the control of our will, e.g. walking, writing, speaking.
  • Involuntary actions — not under the control of our will; they happen automatically, e.g. heartbeat, breathing and movement of food in the alimentary canal; they are regulated by the autonomic nervous system.

Keeping the Brain Healthy

We can keep our brain healthy by eating a balanced diet, taking proper sleep, doing regular exercise, keeping the mind active by reading and learning, and avoiding injuries to the head and harmful substances.

mcqs.why: The reflex arc pathway is: receptor, sensory neuron, inter-neuron (in the spinal cord), motor neuron, effector — so the sensory neuron carries the impulse first.

mcqs.q: In a reflex arc, the inter-neuron is located in the:
mcqs.why: In the reflex arc the inter-neuron is in the spinal cord, which is the centre of reflex actions; it passes the message from the sensory neuron to the motor neuron.

mcqs.why: A reflex action is an immediate, involuntary and automatic response to a stimulus, e.g. pulling the hand away from a hot object.

mcqs.why: Involuntary actions are not under the control of our will and happen automatically, e.g. heartbeat, breathing and movement of food in the alimentary canal.

mcqs.why: The book states that involuntary actions are regulated by the autonomic nervous system, while voluntary actions are controlled by the cerebrum.

mcqs.why: We can keep our brain healthy by eating a balanced diet, taking proper sleep and doing regular exercise; the book lists balanced diet, proper sleep and exercise as all required for brain health.

mcqs.why: The effector (a muscle or gland) gives the response at the end of the reflex arc — in the hot-object example the arm muscle pulls the hand away.

lessons.title: Variation and Adaptation
lessons.notes_html:
Variation is the differences in the characteristics between the individuals of the same species. You are different from your brothers and sisters — this is called variation. Examples of genetic variation: eye colour, attached earlobes and blood group. A mark of a cut on the skin is not a genetic variation.

Benefits of Variation

Variation makes individuals of a species different from one another. It helps a species to adapt to a changing environment and to survive; useful variations are passed to the next generations, so variation is the basis of evolution and of improvement of plants and animals by breeding.

Adaptation

Adaptation is the process by which a species becomes better suited to its environment. Adaptation may be behavioural, structural or physical, and it develops because of useful variations. Example: hibernation helps an animal to escape from cold.

lessons.title: Genes, Chromosomes and DNA
lessons.notes_html:
A gene is a section of DNA which has the information for making a specific protein — it carries information for a particular trait. The term gene was coined by Wilhelm Johannsen (1909).

The word chromosome is derived from a Greek word which means 'colour body'; the term was coined by Heinrich Wilhelm Waldeyer (1888).

Genotype and Phenotype

  • Genotype — the genetic make-up of an organism, i.e. the genes (alleles) present in its cells for a character, e.g. TT or Tt for tallness.
  • Phenotype — the observable characteristic that is actually expressed, e.g. the plant is tall. The phenotype depends on the genotype and the environment.

The Watson and Crick Model of DNA

Watson and Crick proposed that DNA is a double helix — two strands twisted around each other like a twisted ladder. Each strand is made of nucleotides; every nucleotide consists of a pentose sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base. The sugar and phosphate groups form the sides (backbone) of the ladder and the bases form its steps. Adenine always pairs with thymine and guanine with cytosine. DNA stores all the information for the characters of an organism.

Genetics is the branch of biology which deals with heredity — the study of genes and the passing of characteristics from parents to offspring.

mcqs.why: A gene is a section of DNA which carries information for a particular trait, i.e. for making a specific protein.

mcqs.q: The term 'chromosome' is derived from a Greek word which means:
mcqs.why: The book's MCQ answer: chromosome comes from a Greek word meaning 'colour body', because chromosomes absorb coloured stains.

mcqs.q: A nucleotide is composed of a pentose sugar, a phosphate group and a:
mcqs.why: Every nucleotide consists of three parts: a pentose sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base.

mcqs.q: In the DNA double helix, adenine always pairs with:
mcqs.why: Watson and Crick's model: adenine always pairs with thymine and guanine always pairs with cytosine; the base pairs form the steps of the ladder.

mcqs.q: In DNA, guanine always pairs with:
mcqs.why: The base-pairing rule in DNA is A with T and G with C, so guanine always pairs with cytosine.

mcqs.q: Who coined the term 'gene'?
mcqs.why: The term gene was coined by Wilhelm Johannsen in 1909; the term chromosome was coined earlier by Heinrich Wilhelm Waldeyer in 1888.

mcqs.q: Genotype means:
options: The observable characteristic of an organism
The genetic make-up of an organism, e.g. TT or Tt
mcqs.why: Genotype is the genetic make-up — the genes (alleles) present in the cells for a character, e.g. TT or Tt for tallness; the expressed character is the phenotype.

mcqs.why: Phenotype is the observable characteristic that is actually expressed — the plant is tall; the genotype is the allele combination TT or Tt behind it.

lessons.title: How Characteristics Are Passed On: Heredity
lessons.notes_html:
The traits which are passed from parents to offspring are called hereditary characters.

Passing On of Characteristics

Characteristics are passed from parents to offspring through genes present on the chromosomes of the gametes. Male gametes are called sperms and female gametes are called eggs. At fertilisation the sperm and egg fuse, so the offspring receives half of its chromosomes (with genes) from each parent and shows characters of both.

In humans, each sperm and egg has 23 chromosomes, so the fertilised egg has the full 46 chromosomes.

lessons.title: Cell Division: Mitosis and Meiosis
lessons.notes_html:
Cells divide for growth of the organism, for repair and replacement of dead and damaged cells, and for reproduction.

Mitosis

Mitosis is the type of cell division in which one cell divides to form two identical cells and the diploid number of chromosomes remains constant. It takes place in body cells for growth and repair. Before division, in interphase (the preparatory phase), the DNA in the cell is copied — the duplication of chromosomes takes place. Then the division of the nucleus (karyokinesis) takes place in stages — prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase. Finally the division of the cytoplasm, called cytokinesis, divides the cell into two equal daughter cells.

Meiosis

Meiosis is the division by which gametes (sperms and eggs) are formed. It consists of two successive divisions, meiosis-I and meiosis-II. In meiosis-I the reduction of chromosomes takes place: the diploid (2n) number becomes haploid (n). Meiosis-II is similar to mitosis. In this way one parent cell forms four daughter cells, each with half the number of chromosomes; in humans each sperm and egg has 23 chromosomes. Meiosis produces variation in the offspring.

mcqs.why: Mitosis produces two identical daughter cells with the diploid chromosome number unchanged; it takes place in body cells for growth and repair.

mcqs.why: In meiosis-I the reduction of chromosomes takes place: the diploid (2n) number becomes haploid (n); meiosis-II is similar to mitosis.

mcqs.why: Interphase is the preparatory phase before division in which the DNA in the cell is copied — the duplication of chromosomes takes place.

mcqs.why: Cytokinesis is the division of the cytoplasm, which finally divides the cell into two equal daughter cells after the nucleus has divided.

mcqs.why: Meiosis consists of two successive divisions, meiosis-I and meiosis-II, so one parent cell forms four daughter cells, each with half the chromosomes.

mcqs.why: After interphase, the division of the nucleus (karyokinesis) takes place in the stages prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase, followed by cytokinesis.

mcqs.why: Meiosis forms gametes with half the chromosomes and new gene combinations; at fertilisation the offspring receives genes from both parents, so meiosis produces variation.

lessons.title: Biotechnology and Genetic Engineering
lessons.notes_html:
Biotechnology is the use of living organisms, cells or their parts (such as enzymes and genes) to make useful products for human beings, e.g. medicines, foods and fuels. Modern biotechnology uses genetic engineering and recombinant DNA technology to change the genes of organisms for our benefit.

Plasmids and Recombinant DNA

  • The extra rings of DNA in bacteria are called plasmids.
  • A plasmid with an attached foreign gene is collectively called a recombinant plasmid, and the combined DNA is recombinant DNA.
  • The organisms whose cells and plasmids are usually used in genetic engineering are bacteria.

Brewing and baking bread are common examples of fermentation, an old use of microorganisms. GMOs have improved fermentation by enhancing the efficiency of microorganisms.

lessons.title: Making Insulin by Recombinant DNA Technology
lessons.notes_html:
Insulin was the first biotechnology product developed through recombinant DNA technology. Recombinant DNA technology can be used to produce insulin for diabetic patients.

Process of Insulin Production

  • The human insulin gene is cut from human DNA.
  • It is joined with a plasmid (the extra ring of DNA) taken from a bacterium; the plasmid with the attached foreign gene is the recombinant plasmid.
  • These plasmids are mixed with the bacteria E. coli in order to introduce the plasmids into the host cells.
  • The bacteria multiply rapidly and, following the insulin gene, produce human insulin, which is separated and purified.

Synthetic insulin is made in both bacteria and yeast.

lessons.title: Biotechnology in Agriculture and Food
lessons.notes_html:
Applications in Agriculture

In agriculture, biotechnology is used to produce transgenic (genetically modified) crops with more yield, resistance against pests and diseases and better nutritional value. It is also used for biofertilizers, biopesticides and for producing disease-free plants by tissue culture.

  • Transgenic wheat contains more iron, which helps to overcome iron deficiency.
  • Golden rice (transgenic rice) contains extra vitamin A and iron.

Biofertilizers and Biopesticides

Biofertilizers are living microorganisms which increase the fertility of the soil: they fix nitrogen and make nutrients available to plants, they do not cause water pollution like chemical fertilizers, they are cheap and they keep the soil healthy. Chemical fertilizers are largely responsible for water pollution. Biopesticides are pesticides made from living organisms or natural substances; they are safe for humans, animals and the environment.

Food Biotechnology

Fermentation can make food more nutritious, tastier and easier to digest. Cheese is a dairy product that contains both protein and fats. Most flavourings were traditionally extracted from plants. Plant proteins lack some essential amino acids like lysine and cystine; biotechnology adds the missing nutrients to food.

lessons.title: Biotechnology in Health, Biofuels and Daily Life
lessons.notes_html:
Applications in Health

In health, biotechnology is used to produce insulin for diabetic patients, growth hormone, interferons and beta-endorphin, and vaccines — a preparation that is used to stimulate the body's immune response against diseases. It is also used in making antibiotics and in diagnosing and treating inherited diseases. Quinine is not a biotechnological product — it is a natural product from plants.

Biofuels

Biofuels are fuels obtained from living matter (plants and microorganisms). Their advantages are: they are renewable, they produce less pollution than fossil fuels, they reduce our dependence on coal and petroleum, and the raw material (crops and waste) is easily available.

Bioplastic and Cultivated Meat

Bioplastic is a plastic material produced from renewable biological sources such as plants (corn starch, sugarcane) and microorganisms instead of petroleum. It is biodegradable, so it does not pollute the environment like ordinary plastic. Cultivated meat (lab meat) is meat produced in the laboratory by growing animal cells in a culture medium, without slaughtering animals.

Enzymatic Detergents

A detergent is a substance used for cleaning clothes and utensils. Enzymatic detergents contain enzymes obtained through biotechnology; the enzymes break down stains of protein, fat and starch, so clothes are cleaned better even at low temperature and with less water and energy.

Biotechnology in Pakistan

In Pakistan biotechnology is applied in Bt cotton and improved crops, tissue culture, biofertilizers and biopesticides, the health sector (insulin, vaccines, diagnostic kits), fermentation industries and treatment of waste water. Research is carried out in institutes such as NIBGE and CEMB.

lessons.title: Groups and Periods of the Periodic Table
lessons.notes_html:
In the periodic table, elements are arranged in the order of increasing atomic numbers.

Groups

The vertical columns of elements in the periodic table are called groups. There are 18 groups. Elements in the same group have similar chemical properties due to the same number of valence electrons. Family names:

  • Group 1 — alkali metals
  • Group 17 — halogens
  • Group 18 — noble gases

Periods

The horizontal rows of the periodic table are called periods. There are 7 periods. The number of elements in each period is: 1st period 2, 2nd period 8, 3rd period 8, 4th period 18, 5th period 18, 6th period 32 (the longest) and 7th period 32 (incomplete). Elements in the same period have different chemical properties because they have different numbers of valence electrons.

lessons.title: The First 18 Elements and Electronic Configuration
lessons.notes_html:
The First 18 Elements

1 Hydrogen, 2 Helium, 3 Lithium, 4 Beryllium, 5 Boron, 6 Carbon, 7 Nitrogen, 8 Oxygen, 9 Fluorine, 10 Neon, 11 Sodium, 12 Magnesium, 13 Aluminium, 14 Silicon, 15 Phosphorus, 16 Sulphur, 17 Chlorine, 18 Argon.

The Second Period

The second period contains 8 elements: Lithium, Beryllium, Boron, Carbon, Nitrogen, Oxygen, Fluorine and Neon. The third period also contains eight (8) elements.

Finding Group and Period

  • Phosphorus has atomic number 15. Its electronic configuration is 2,8,5; it has 5 valence electrons, so it is in group 15, and it has 3 shells, so it is in period 3.
  • Oxygen has atomic number 8 and configuration 2,6, so it has 6 valence electrons (group 16).
  • Nitrogen (2,5) and Phosphorus (2,8,5) have five electrons in the outermost shell; they belong to group 15.
  • Examples by group: Group 2 — Magnesium (or Calcium); Group 15 — Nitrogen (or Phosphorus); Group 18 — Neon (or Argon), a noble gas.

Lithium, sodium and magnesium are all metals.

lessons.title: Metals: Properties and Uses
lessons.notes_html:
Properties of Metals

  • They are lustrous (shiny).
  • They are malleable (can be beaten into sheets) and ductile (can be drawn into wires).
  • They are sonorous — they produce a ringing sound when struck.
  • They have high tensile strength — the property of a metal to bear a load before it stretches or breaks.
  • They are good conductors of heat and electricity.

Uses of Metals

  • Iron — used in making nails, bolts, machinery and tools, and in construction, because of its high tensile strength and durability.
  • Copper — used for making electric wires and cables because it is a very good conductor of electricity and is ductile.
  • Gold — used in jewellery and coins because it is lustrous and does not corrode.
  • Platinum — used in jewellery, in laboratory equipment and as a catalyst in industries.
  • Mercury — used in thermometers; it is the metal which is liquid at room temperature.
  • Silver — used in jewellery.

School bells are made of metals because metals are sonorous; a bell of a non-metal would not ring.

lessons.title: Non-metals: Properties and Uses
lessons.notes_html:
Properties of Non-metals

Non-metals are the elements which are non-malleable, non-ductile, brittle, non-sonorous, and poor conductors of heat and electricity. They are dull, without lustre. The characteristic property of non-metals is brittleness.

States of Non-metals

  • Solid non-metals: carbon and sulphur (phosphorus and iodine are also solids).
  • Bromine is the only non-metal which is liquid at room temperature.
  • Gaseous non-metals: hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen and chlorine (fluorine and the noble gases are also gases).

An Exception

Graphite (a form of carbon) is a non-metal that is a good conductor of electricity. At room temperature, mercury (a metal) exists in liquid state, while graphite is a non-metal which is a good conductor of electricity.

Matching Uses

  • Silicon — electronic devices
  • Graphite — lead pencil
  • Oxygen — respiration

mcqs.why: Graphite is the exception: although a non-metal (a form of carbon), it is a good conductor of electricity and is used in electrodes and pencils.

mcqs.why: The book's matching answers: silicon — electronic devices, oxygen — respiration, iron — machinery and tools, silver — jewellery.

mcqs.q: In the matching exercise, oxygen is matched with:
mcqs.why: Oxygen is matched with respiration; the extra Column B entry 'Food container' has no match because aluminium is not listed in Column A.

mcqs.q: Non-metals are described as dull because they:
mcqs.why: Non-metals are dull, without lustre, non-sonorous and brittle — the opposite of metals in each of these properties.

lessons.title: Chemical Reactions, Reactants and Products
lessons.notes_html:
A chemical reaction is the transformation of one chemical substance into another; a new substance is formed with different composition and properties than the original substances. The starting substances are called reactants and the new substances formed are called products.

Chemical Equations

A chemical equation is a mathematical statement that symbolizes the formation of products from reactants, using the symbols and formulae of the substances, e.g. 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O. The reactants are written on the left hand side and the products on the right hand side.

Law of Conservation of Mass

The law of conservation of mass states that in a chemical reaction the total mass of the reactants equals the total mass of the products. Matter is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction; the atoms are only rearranged. This is why a chemical equation must be balanced, with the same number of atoms of each element on both sides.

Is Fire a Chemical Reaction?

Yes — fire is a combustion reaction in which a fuel reacts with oxygen and produces new substances (carbon dioxide, water vapour, ash) with the release of heat and light energy. Examples of chemical reactions: burning of methane, rusting of iron, and the reaction of zinc with copper sulphate solution.

mcqs.q: In a chemical reaction, the substances that react together are called:
mcqs.why: The starting substances in a chemical reaction are called reactants; the new substances formed are called products.

mcqs.q: What does the Law of Conservation of Mass state?
options: Energy cannot be created or destroyed
The total mass of reactants equals the total mass of products
The total energy in a system remains constant
mcqs.why: In a chemical reaction matter is neither created nor destroyed; the atoms are only rearranged, so the total mass of reactants equals the total mass of products.

mcqs.q: In a balanced chemical equation, the number and type of atoms:
options: Are only equal on the product side
Are only equal on the reactant side
Must be equal on both sides
mcqs.why: A chemical equation must be balanced because of the law of conservation of mass: the number and type of atoms must be equal on both sides.

mcqs.q: Reactants are written on which side of a chemical equation?
mcqs.why: The fill-in-the-blank answer in the book: reactants are the substances written on the left hand side of the equation; products are on the right.

mcqs.q: A chemical equation is:
options: A mathematical statement that symbolizes the formation of products from reactants
mcqs.why: A chemical equation symbolizes the formation of products from reactants using symbols and formulae, e.g. 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O.

mcqs.q: Is fire a chemical reaction?
options: No, because nothing new is formed
Yes, it is a combustion reaction forming new substances with heat and light
No, it is only a physical change
Yes, but no energy is released
mcqs.why: Fire is a combustion reaction: a fuel reacts with oxygen and produces new substances (carbon dioxide, water vapour, ash) with the release of heat and light.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an example of a chemical reaction given in the book?
mcqs.why: Rusting of iron forms a new substance, so it is a chemical reaction; melting and boiling are physical changes with no new substance.

mcqs.q: In a chemical reaction, the atoms of the reactants are:
mcqs.why: Matter is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction; the atoms are only rearranged into the products, which is why equations are balanced.

mcqs.q: The new substances formed in a chemical reaction are called:
mcqs.why: The starting substances are reactants and the new substances formed are products, written on the right hand side of the equation.

mcqs.q: Besides burning of methane and rusting of iron, the book gives which other example of a chemical reaction?
options: The reaction of zinc with copper sulphate solution
mcqs.why: The book's examples of chemical reactions are burning of methane, rusting of iron, and the reaction of zinc with copper sulphate solution.

lessons.title: Types of Reactions: Combination, Displacement and Combustion
lessons.notes_html:
Combination Reaction

Two or more substances combine to form one product, e.g. 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O and CaO + H2O → Ca(OH)2.

Single Displacement Reaction

A more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its compound. Example: zinc is more reactive than copper, so when zinc is dipped into copper sulphate solution it displaces the copper; the blue colour of the solution fades and a brown coating of copper is deposited on the zinc:

Zn + CuSO4 → ZnSO4 + Cu

Potassium reacting with magnesium chloride is also a single displacement reaction. Carbon displacing lead from lead oxide (2PbO + C → 2Pb + CO2) is another example.

Double Displacement Reaction

Two compounds exchange their ions to form two new compounds, e.g. BaCl2 + CuSO4 → BaSO4 + CuCl2 (a precipitate of BaSO4 is formed), and NaCl + AgNO3 → NaNO3 + AgCl.

Combustion Reaction

A combustion reaction is a reaction in which a substance burns in oxygen (or air) and produces heat and light energy, e.g. CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O. The burning of ethyne (2C2H2 + 5O2 → 4CO2 + 2H2O) is also combustion.

mcqs.q: What type of reaction occurs when potassium reacts with magnesium chloride?
mcqs.why: Potassium is more reactive than magnesium, so it displaces magnesium from its compound — a single displacement reaction.

mcqs.q: Which type of reaction involves the exchange of ions between two compounds?
mcqs.why: In a double displacement reaction two compounds exchange their ions to form two new compounds, e.g. BaCl2 + CuSO4 → BaSO4 + CuCl2.

mcqs.q: Which of the following reactions is a combination reaction?
mcqs.why: In 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O two substances combine to form one product; the AgNO3 reaction is double displacement and the methane reaction is combustion.

mcqs.q: When zinc is dipped into copper sulphate solution, what is observed?
options: The blue colour fades and a brown coating of copper forms on the zinc
mcqs.why: Zinc is more reactive than copper, so it displaces copper from copper sulphate; the blue colour fades and brown copper is deposited on the zinc.

mcqs.q: The reaction Zn + CuSO4 → ZnSO4 + Cu is an example of:
mcqs.why: Zinc alone displaces copper from its compound, forming zinc sulphate and copper — a single displacement reaction.

mcqs.q: CaO + H2O → Ca(OH)2 represents which type of reaction?
mcqs.why: Two substances, CaO and H2O, combine to form one product, Ca(OH)2 — a combination reaction.

mcqs.q: BaCl2 + CuSO4 → BaSO4 + CuCl2 is which type of reaction?
mcqs.why: The two compounds exchange their ions and a precipitate of BaSO4 is formed — a double displacement reaction.

mcqs.q: A combustion reaction is a reaction in which a substance:
options: Burns in oxygen and produces heat and light energy
mcqs.why: In combustion a substance burns in oxygen (or air) and produces heat and light energy, e.g. methane burning to give carbon dioxide and water.

mcqs.q: The burning of ethyne, 2C2H2 + 5O2 → 4CO2 + 2H2O, is a:
mcqs.why: Ethyne burns in oxygen producing heat and light, so the reaction is a combustion reaction, as classified in the book.

mcqs.q: In a single displacement reaction, the displacing element must be:
options: Less reactive than the element it replaces
More reactive than the element it displaces
mcqs.why: A more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its compound — zinc displaces copper, and carbon displaces lead from lead oxide.

lessons.title: Exothermic and Endothermic Reactions
lessons.notes_html:
Exothermic Reactions

Exothermic reactions release energy to the surroundings, e.g. combustion and the oxidation of glucose. The reaction of methane with oxygen to produce carbon dioxide and water is an exothermic reaction:

CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O + energy

Endothermic Reactions

Endothermic reactions absorb energy from the surroundings. The reaction in which energy is absorbed is known as an endothermic reaction. The main example is photosynthesis:

6CO2 + 6H2O + energy (sunlight) → C6H12O6 + 6O2

Check for the photosynthesis equation: C 6 = 6; H 12 = 12; O 18 = 18 on both sides — it is balanced. Melting of ice also takes in heat, while sweating cools the body by evaporation; neither is the book's main example of an exothermic reaction — that is the oxidation of glucose.

mcqs.q: What is the main example of an exothermic reaction given in the book?
mcqs.why: The oxidation of glucose releases energy in the body, so it is the book's main example of an exothermic reaction; photosynthesis is endothermic.

mcqs.q: The reaction in which energy is absorbed is known as an:
mcqs.why: The fill-in-the-blank answer in the book: the reaction in which energy is absorbed is an endothermic reaction; reactions releasing energy are exothermic.

mcqs.q: The reaction of methane with oxygen to produce carbon dioxide and water is an example of an:
mcqs.why: Burning methane releases heat and light energy to the surroundings, so it is an exothermic (combustion) reaction.

mcqs.q: Photosynthesis is an endothermic reaction because it:
mcqs.why: In photosynthesis plants absorb energy from sunlight to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen: 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy → C6H12O6 + 6O2.

mcqs.q: Which is the correct balanced equation for photosynthesis?
mcqs.why: Counting atoms: 6CO2 + 6H2O → C6H12O6 + 6O2 gives C 6 = 6, H 12 = 12 and O 18 = 18 on both sides, so it is balanced.

mcqs.q: An exothermic reaction is one which:
mcqs.why: Exothermic reactions release energy, e.g. combustion and oxidation of glucose; endothermic reactions absorb energy, e.g. photosynthesis.

mcqs.q: In the exothermic equation CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O + energy, the energy appears on the:
options: Reactant side, because it is absorbed
Product side, because it is released
It should not appear at all
mcqs.why: Burning methane releases energy, so energy is written with the products; in endothermic photosynthesis, energy (sunlight) is written with the reactants.

mcqs.q: Combustion reactions are exothermic because they:
mcqs.why: A combustion reaction burns a substance in oxygen and produces heat and light energy, releasing energy to the surroundings — the mark of an exothermic reaction.

mcqs.q: Melting of ice takes in heat from the surroundings, so it is a process of the type called:
mcqs.why: Processes that absorb energy from the surroundings are endothermic; melting of ice absorbs heat, unlike the oxidation of glucose which releases energy.

mcqs.q: In an endothermic reaction, the absorbed energy is written in the equation:
options: Only under the arrow as a catalyst
mcqs.why: In photosynthesis the absorbed sunlight is written with the reactants: 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy (sunlight) → C6H12O6 + 6O2.

lessons.title: Balancing Equations and Chemical Bonds
lessons.notes_html:
Rules for Balancing Chemical Equations

  • Write the correct formulae of reactants and products.
  • Count the atoms of each element on both sides.
  • Balance one element at a time by putting suitable numbers (coefficients) in front of the formulae, starting with metals, then non-metals, and hydrogen and oxygen last.
  • Never change the formula (subscripts) of a substance.
  • Finally check every element again.

Worked Examples

  • 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO (Mg 2 = 2, O 2 = 2)
  • 2H2O2 → 2H2O + O2 (MnO2 is a catalyst and is not consumed)
  • 4P + 5O2 → 2P2O5 (P 4 = 4, O 10 = 10)
  • 2Pb(NO3)2 → 2PbO + 4NO2 + O2 (Pb 2, N 4, O 12 on both sides)
  • CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O (C 1, H 4, O 4 on both sides)

Ionic and Covalent Bonds

Atoms are held together in a molecule by chemical bonds. An ionic bond is formed by the transfer of electrons from a metal atom to a non-metal atom; the oppositely charged ions attract each other by electrostatic forces, e.g. sodium (2,8,1) transfers its valence electron to chlorine (2,8,7), forming Na+ and Cl− in sodium chloride. Sodium and oxygen will most likely form an ionic bond. An ionic bond cannot form between two metals, because both tend to lose electrons. A covalent bond is formed by the sharing of electrons between atoms, typically between non-metals, e.g. CH4 and CO2. Prefixes (mono-, di-, tri-) are used to indicate the number of atoms in the formula of a covalent compound: CO2 is carbon dioxide.

Magnesium Oxide

Magnesium (2,8,2) has 2 valence electrons. In magnesium oxide it loses both and attains the structure 2,8 — the noble gas structure of neon — forming Mg2+, while oxygen (2,6) gains them to form O2−.

mcqs.q: What type of bond is formed by the sharing of electrons between atoms?
mcqs.why: A covalent bond is formed by the sharing of electrons between atoms; an ionic bond is formed by the transfer of electrons.

mcqs.q: What is the correct systematic name for CO2?
mcqs.why: Prefixes indicate the number of atoms in a covalent compound: CO2 has two oxygen atoms, so it is carbon dioxide (di- = two).

mcqs.q: Atoms are held together in a molecule by:
mcqs.why: The fill-in-the-blank answer in the book: atoms are held together in a molecule by chemical bonds — ionic bonds by transfer and covalent bonds by sharing of electrons.

mcqs.q: Sodium and oxygen will most likely form which bond?
mcqs.why: Sodium is a metal and oxygen a non-metal; the fill-in answer is 'ionic' — the metal transfers electrons to the non-metal, forming oppositely charged ions.

mcqs.q: Prefixes are used to indicate the number of atoms present in the formula of which compound?
mcqs.why: Prefixes such as mono-, di- and tri- are used in naming covalent compounds, e.g. carbon dioxide for CO2.

mcqs.q: Balance this equation: Mg + O2 → MgO. The balanced form is:
mcqs.why: Counting atoms: first put 2 before MgO to balance oxygen (O 2 = 2), then 2 before Mg (Mg 2 = 2): 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO.

mcqs.q: Balance: P + O2 → P2O5. The balanced equation is:
mcqs.why: Use 5O2 and 2P2O5 to make O 10 = 10; then phosphorus on the right is 4, so put 4 before P: 4P + 5O2 → 2P2O5 (P 4 = 4, O 10 = 10).

mcqs.q: In the decomposition 2H2O2 → 2H2O + O2 over MnO2, the MnO2 is:
options: A catalyst that is not consumed
mcqs.why: MnO2 is written over the arrow as a catalyst: check H 4 = 4 and O 4 = 2 + 2 = 4; the catalyst speeds the reaction and is not consumed.

mcqs.q: What kind of force is present in ionic bonds?
mcqs.why: An electrostatic force of attraction holds the oppositely charged ions together in an ionic bond, e.g. Na+ and Cl− in sodium chloride.

mcqs.q: Magnesium has electron structure 2,8,2. How many valence electrons does it have, and which noble gas structure does it attain in MgO?
mcqs.why: Magnesium's outermost shell (2,8,2) has 2 valence electrons; losing both in MgO leaves 2,8 — the noble gas structure of neon.

lessons.title: Acids and Their Properties
lessons.notes_html:
An acid is a substance that gives hydrogen ions (H+) when dissolved in water. Examples: hydrochloric acid (HCl) and sulphuric acid (H2SO4); citric acid in lemon and acetic acid in vinegar are natural acids.

Physical Properties of Acids

  • They have a sour taste.
  • They turn blue litmus red.
  • Their pH is less than 7.
  • They are usually liquids (some, like citric and tartaric acid, are solids).
  • Their solutions conduct electricity because they produce ions in water.
  • Many concentrated mineral acids are corrosive.

Acid in Our Stomach

Hydrochloric acid (HCl) is the mineral acid present in our stomach. It helps in digestion of food and kills germs, but its excess causes acidity, which is treated with a mild base such as magnesium hydroxide, Mg(OH)2.

Why Sulphuric Acid Shows Acidic Character in Water

Sulphuric acid shows acidic characters in water because in aqueous solution it ionizes and produces hydrogen ions: H2SO4 → 2H+ + SO42−. It is the hydrogen ions which give an acid its acidic properties, so dry sulphuric acid does not show acidic behaviour.

Uses of Common Acids

  • Sulphuric acid — car batteries, fertilizers, detergents and paints.
  • Hydrochloric acid — cleaning metals; digestion in the stomach.
  • Nitric acid — fertilizers and explosives.
  • Acetic acid (vinegar) — food preservation and flavouring.
  • Citric acid — food and drinks.

mcqs.q: A substance that gives hydrogen ions in water is called:
mcqs.why: An acid is a substance that gives hydrogen ions (H+) when dissolved in water; it is these ions that give acids their properties.

mcqs.q: A solution that turns blue litmus red is expected to have a pH of:
mcqs.why: Blue litmus turning red shows the solution is acidic, so its pH is less than 7 — pH 3 fits; 8, 10 and 14 are basic.

mcqs.q: Which acid is present in our stomach?
mcqs.why: Hydrochloric acid (HCl) is the mineral acid present in our stomach; it helps digestion and kills germs, and its excess causes acidity.

mcqs.q: Sulphuric acid shows acidic character in aqueous solution because it produces:
mcqs.why: In water, sulphuric acid ionizes: H2SO4 → 2H+ + SO4^2−. The hydrogen ions give the acid its acidic properties, so dry acid shows no acidic behaviour.

mcqs.q: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Acids have a pH greater than bases
An acid will turn universal indicator blue
An acid can neutralize a base
An acid has a pH greater than 7
mcqs.why: An acid can neutralize a base to form a salt and water; acids have pH less than 7 and turn blue litmus red.

mcqs.q: Acids have which taste?
mcqs.why: Acids have a sour taste, turn blue litmus red and have pH less than 7; bases have a bitter taste and feel soapy.

mcqs.q: What colour does blue litmus paper show in acetic acid solution?
mcqs.why: Acetic acid is an acid, so it turns blue litmus paper red; red litmus paper shows no change in an acid.

mcqs.q: Sulphuric acid is used in:
mcqs.why: Sulphuric acid is used in car batteries and in making fertilizers, detergents and paints; it is also matched in the book as the strong acid used in car batteries.

mcqs.q: A strong acid is one which:
options: Ionizes completely in water and produces many hydrogen ions
mcqs.why: A strong acid ionizes completely in water and produces a large number of hydrogen ions, e.g. hydrochloric acid and sulphuric acid; it has a very low pH.

mcqs.q: An acid is a substance that gives which ions when dissolved in water?
mcqs.why: The fill-in-the-blank answer in the book: an acid gives hydrogen (H+) ions when dissolved in water; bases give hydroxide ions.

lessons.title: Bases, Alkalis and Their Properties
lessons.notes_html:
A base is a substance which neutralizes an acid to form a salt and water only. Bases are metal oxides, metal hydroxides or ammonia. Bases give hydroxide ions (OH−) in water.

Alkalis

The bases which are soluble in water are called alkalis. Examples: sodium hydroxide (NaOH) and potassium hydroxide (KOH); calcium hydroxide (slaked lime) is also an alkali. Sodium hydroxide solution contains the ions Na+ and OH−: NaOH → Na+ + OH−.

Physical Properties of Bases

  • They have a bitter taste.
  • They feel soapy or slippery to touch.
  • They turn red litmus blue.
  • Their pH is greater than 7.
  • Their solutions conduct electricity.
  • Strong bases are corrosive and harmful for the skin.

Uses of Common Bases

  • Sodium hydroxide — making soaps, detergents and paper.
  • Calcium hydroxide (slaked lime) — whitewashing and treating acidic soil; it is basic in nature.
  • Magnesium hydroxide, Mg(OH)2 — used as an antacid to reduce acidity in the stomach.
  • Ammonium hydroxide — making fertilizers.
  • Sodium carbonate (washing soda) — washing clothes.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is basic in nature?
mcqs.why: Slaked lime is calcium hydroxide, a base; lemon, apple and orange juices contain acids and are acidic in nature.

mcqs.q: Which base is used to reduce acidity in the stomach?
mcqs.why: Magnesium hydroxide, Mg(OH)2, is a mild base used as an antacid to neutralize the excess hydrochloric acid in the stomach.

mcqs.q: The bases which are soluble in water are called:
mcqs.why: Bases soluble in water are called alkalis; an alkali gives hydroxide ions (OH−) in solution, e.g. NaOH and KOH.

mcqs.q: The ions present in a solution of sodium hydroxide are:
mcqs.why: Sodium hydroxide is an alkali; in solution it gives sodium ions (Na+) and hydroxide ions (OH−): NaOH → Na+ + OH−.

mcqs.q: Bases turn red litmus:
mcqs.why: Bases turn red litmus blue, feel soapy to touch, have a bitter taste and pH greater than 7 — the opposite litmus change to acids.

mcqs.q: The common name of sodium carbonate is:
mcqs.why: The fill-in-the-blank answer in the book: the common name of sodium carbonate is washing soda; it is used for washing clothes.

mcqs.q: A strong base is one which:
options: Ionizes completely in water and produces many hydroxide ions
mcqs.why: A strong base ionizes completely in water and produces a large number of hydroxide ions, e.g. sodium hydroxide and potassium hydroxide; it has a very high pH.

mcqs.q: Sodium hydroxide is used in making:
mcqs.why: Uses of common bases: sodium hydroxide — soaps, detergents and paper; calcium hydroxide — whitewashing and treating acidic soil; ammonium hydroxide — fertilizers.

mcqs.q: Bases feel ______ to touch.
mcqs.why: Bases feel soapy or slippery to touch, have a bitter taste, turn red litmus blue and have pH greater than 7.

mcqs.q: Calcium hydroxide (slaked lime) is used for:
mcqs.why: Slaked lime is used in whitewashing and for treating acidic soil, because as a base it neutralizes the acidity of the soil.

lessons.title: The pH Scale and Indicators
lessons.notes_html:
pH

pH is a measure of the strength (acidity or alkalinity) of a solution — the pH scale measures the strength of acids and bases in a solution. Its range is from 0 to 14:

  • pH 7 is neutral.
  • pH less than 7 is acidic — the lower the pH, the stronger the acid.
  • pH greater than 7 is basic or alkaline — the higher the pH, the stronger the base; the higher the pH of a solution, the higher is the alkalinity of the solution.

Indicators

Indicators are chemicals that identify substances as acidic, basic or neutral by showing different colours in acidic and basic solutions.

  • Natural indicators: litmus, a common natural indicator extracted from plant lichens (blue litmus and red litmus); red cabbage juice and turmeric are also natural indicators.
  • Synthetic indicators used in labs: methyl orange and phenolphthalein.
  • Universal indicator is a mixture of indicators that displays a range of colours depending on the strength of acids and bases.

mcqs.q: The range of the pH scale is:
mcqs.why: pH is a measure of the strength of acids and bases; its range is from 0 to 14, with 7 neutral, below 7 acidic and above 7 basic.

mcqs.q: A solution whose pH is less than 7 is ______ in nature.
mcqs.why: The fill-in-the-blank answer in the book: a solution whose pH is less than 7 is acidic in nature; the lower the pH, the stronger the acid.

mcqs.q: The higher the pH of a solution, the higher is its:
mcqs.why: The fill-in-the-blank answer in the book: the higher the pH, the higher is the alkalinity of the solution.

mcqs.q: A neutral solution has a pH of exactly:
mcqs.why: A pH of 7 is neutral; pH less than 7 is acidic and pH greater than 7 is basic or alkaline.

mcqs.q: Red cabbage juice is a ______ indicator.
mcqs.why: Red cabbage juice is a natural indicator, like litmus (from lichens) and turmeric; methyl orange and phenolphthalein are synthetic indicators.

mcqs.q: Litmus, the common natural indicator, is extracted from:
mcqs.why: Litmus is a natural indicator extracted from plant lichens; it comes in two types, blue litmus and red litmus.

mcqs.q: Which of the following are synthetic indicators used in labs?
mcqs.why: Methyl orange and phenolphthalein are synthetic indicators made in laboratories; litmus, red cabbage juice and turmeric are natural indicators.

mcqs.q: Universal indicator is:
options: A mixture of indicators showing a range of colours with pH
mcqs.why: Universal indicator is a mixture of indicators that displays a range of colours depending on the strength of acids and bases.

mcqs.q: Indicators identify substances as acidic, basic or neutral by:
options: Showing different colours in acidic and basic solutions
mcqs.why: Indicators are chemicals that show different colours in acidic and basic solutions, e.g. blue litmus turns red in acid and red litmus turns blue in a base.

mcqs.q: Which solution is the most strongly basic?
mcqs.why: The higher the pH above 7, the stronger the base; pH 14 is the most strongly basic of the choices, while pH 7 is neutral.

lessons.title: Neutralization, Salts and Acids in Daily Life
lessons.notes_html:
Neutralization

When an acid is added to a base, the acid neutralizes the base and a salt and water are formed. This is called a neutralization reaction:

Acid + Base → Salt + Water

  • HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O
  • NaOH + HNO3 → NaNO3 + H2O (sodium nitrate)
  • H2SO4 + Mg(OH)2 → MgSO4 + 2H2O (magnesium sulphate)

A salt consists of a cation from the base and an anion from the acid.

Salts: Properties and Uses

Most salts are solids at room temperature, usually crystalline, with high melting and boiling points. Many are soluble in water, though some (like BaSO4 and CaCO3) are insoluble. Their solutions and molten forms conduct electricity. Uses: sodium chloride (common salt) in food and preserving food; sodium carbonate (washing soda) for washing and in the glass industry; calcium carbonate in cement and building material (limestone and marble); copper sulphate as a fungicide in agriculture. Sulphuric acid (H2SO4) is the strong acid used in car batteries, and calcium carbonate (CaCO3) is the main component of limestone and marble.

Organic and Mineral Acids

  • Organic acids — obtained from living organisms; generally weak. Citric acid (lemon, orange), lactic acid (milk/curd), acetic acid (vinegar), formic acid (bee sting), tartaric acid (grapes), oxalic acid (spinach).
  • Mineral acids — prepared from minerals in the laboratory or industry; generally strong. Hydrochloric, sulphuric and nitric acids.

An acid present in the stings of bees is formic acid. Lactic acid is present in milk (curd) and citric acid in lemon.

mcqs.q: A neutralization reaction occurs between:
mcqs.why: Neutralization occurs between an acid and a base, producing a salt and water: Acid + Base → Salt + Water.

mcqs.q: What happens when an acid is added to a base?
options: A salt and water are formed
mcqs.why: The acid neutralizes the base and a salt and water are formed, e.g. HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O.

mcqs.q: The salt formed when sodium hydroxide reacts with nitric acid is:
mcqs.why: NaOH + HNO3 → NaNO3 + H2O: the salt is sodium nitrate, made of the cation from the base (Na+) and the anion from the acid (NO3−).

mcqs.q: H2SO4 + Mg(OH)2 → MgSO4 + 2H2O. The salt formed is:
mcqs.why: Sulphuric acid with magnesium hydroxide gives magnesium sulphate and water — a neutralization reaction; check: H 4 = 4, O 6 = 6 on both sides.

mcqs.q: An acid present in the stings of bees is:
mcqs.why: The book's MCQ answer: formic acid is present in bee stings; lactic acid is in curd, acetic acid in vinegar and oxalic acid in spinach.

mcqs.q: Lactic acid is present in ______ and citric acid in ______.
mcqs.why: Lactic acid is present in milk (curd) and citric acid is present in lemon, as given in the book's short answers and matching exercise.

mcqs.q: In the matching exercise, tartaric acid is matched with:
mcqs.why: The book's matching answers: acetic acid — vinegar, lactic acid — curd, tartaric acid — grapes, oxalic acid — spinach, citric acid — orange.

mcqs.q: Organic acids are generally ______ and mineral acids are generally ______.
mcqs.why: Organic acids from living organisms (citric, lactic, acetic) are generally weak, while mineral acids prepared from minerals (hydrochloric, sulphuric, nitric) are generally strong.

mcqs.q: A salt formed in neutralization consists of:
options: A cation from the acid and an anion from the base
A cation from the base and an anion from the acid
mcqs.why: A salt consists of a cation from the base and an anion from the acid, e.g. in NaCl the Na+ comes from NaOH and the Cl− from HCl.

mcqs.q: Copper sulphate is used in agriculture as a:
mcqs.why: Uses of salts from the book: copper sulphate is used as a fungicide in agriculture; common salt preserves food and calcium carbonate is used in cement.

chapters.title: Unit 8: Reflection and Refraction of Light

lessons.title: Light, Media and the Speed of Light
lessons.notes_html:
Light is a form of energy which produces the sensation of vision; it enables us to see objects.

Basic Properties of Light

  • It travels in straight lines.
  • Its speed in space (vacuum) is 3 × 108 m/s (300,000 km/s) — the maximum speed; the speed of light depends upon the medium.
  • In a denser medium the speed of light decreases, e.g. in glass and water; it is greatest in space.
  • It undergoes reflection and refraction.
  • White light is a mixture of seven colours.

Media

  • A transparent medium allows light to pass through it, e.g. water, glass and air.
  • A translucent medium allows light to pass only partially, so objects cannot be seen clearly through it, e.g. frosted glass and tracing paper.
  • A rarer medium is one in which light travels faster, e.g. air and space; a denser medium is one in which the speed of light decreases, e.g. water and glass.

Transmission and Absorption

Transmission is the passing of light through a medium. Absorption is the taking in (soaking up) of light by a surface or medium: a black surface absorbs all the colours of light, while a white surface reflects all the colours.

mcqs.q: The value of the speed of light in space is:
mcqs.why: The fill-in answer in the book: the speed of light in space is 3 × 10^8 m/s (300,000 km/s), the maximum speed.

mcqs.q: In a denser medium, the speed of light:
mcqs.why: The speed of light decreases in a denser medium such as glass or water; it is greatest in space (vacuum).

mcqs.q: The speed of light is greater in which medium?
mcqs.why: Light travels fastest in space (vacuum); its speed decreases in air, water and glass, in that order.

mcqs.q: The speed of light depends upon:
mcqs.why: The fill-in-the-blank answer in the book: the speed of light depends upon the medium through which it travels.

mcqs.q: Water is an example of which medium?
mcqs.why: Water is a transparent medium — light passes through it and objects can be seen clearly; frosted glass is translucent.

mcqs.q: A translucent medium, e.g. frosted glass, allows light to pass:
options: Only partially, so objects cannot be seen clearly
mcqs.why: A translucent medium allows light to pass through it only partially, so objects cannot be seen clearly through it, e.g. frosted glass and tracing paper.

mcqs.q: Which colours are absorbed by a black surface?
mcqs.why: A black surface absorbs all the colours of light and none is reflected — that is why it looks black; a white surface reflects all colours.

mcqs.q: Which colours are reflected by a white surface?
mcqs.why: A white surface reflects all the colours of white light; a black surface absorbs all of them.

mcqs.q: Absorption of light means:
options: Passing of light through a medium
Taking in (soaking up) of light by a surface or medium
mcqs.why: Absorption is the taking in of light by a surface or medium, e.g. a black surface absorbs all colours; transmission is the passing of light through a medium.

mcqs.q: Light travels in:
mcqs.why: A basic property of light is that it travels in straight lines; it also undergoes reflection and refraction and can be dispersed into seven colours.

lessons.title: Reflection of Light and the Plane Mirror
lessons.notes_html:
Reflection of light is the bouncing back of light when it strikes a surface.

Laws of Reflection

  • The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane.
  • The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection (∠i = ∠r).

The normal line is the line drawn perpendicular (at 90°) to the reflecting surface at the point where the light ray strikes it. The angle between the normal and the reflected ray is called the angle of reflection.

Regular and Diffuse Reflection

  • Regular reflection takes place from a smooth and polished surface (like a plane mirror); the reflected rays remain parallel and a clear image is formed.
  • Diffuse (irregular) reflection takes place from a rough surface; the reflected rays scatter in different directions and no image is formed, although the surface becomes visible.

Image in a Plane Mirror

A plane mirror forms an image which is virtual, erect, of the same size as the object, and as far behind the mirror as the object is in front of it. The image is laterally inverted — the left side of the object appears as the right side of the image.

mcqs.q: For a plane mirror, which relation is true for the angle of incidence (i) and angle of reflection (r)?
mcqs.why: By the laws of reflection, the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection (∠i = ∠r) for every mirror, including a plane mirror.

mcqs.q: The angle between the normal and the reflected ray is called the:
mcqs.why: The fill-in-the-blank answer in the book: the angle between the normal and the reflected ray is the angle of reflection; the angle with the incident ray is the angle of incidence.

mcqs.q: The normal line is drawn at what angle to the surface?
mcqs.why: The normal line is drawn perpendicular (at 90 degrees) to the reflecting or refracting surface at the point where the light ray strikes it.

mcqs.q: Regular reflection takes place from:
mcqs.why: Regular reflection occurs at a smooth, polished surface like a plane mirror, where reflected rays remain parallel and a clear image is formed.

mcqs.q: In diffuse reflection, the reflected rays:
options: Scatter in different directions and no image is formed
mcqs.why: Diffuse (irregular) reflection takes place from a rough surface; the reflected rays scatter in different directions and no image is formed.

mcqs.q: The image formed by a plane mirror is:
options: Virtual, erect and of the same size as the object
mcqs.why: A plane mirror forms a virtual, erect image of the same size as the object, as far behind the mirror as the object is in front, and laterally inverted.

mcqs.q: Laterally inverted means that in the mirror image:
options: The left side of the object appears as the right side of the image
mcqs.why: Lateral inversion: the left side of the object appears as the right side of the image in a plane mirror, e.g. writing appears reversed.

mcqs.q: According to the laws of reflection, the incident ray, reflected ray and normal all lie in:
mcqs.why: First law of reflection: the incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane.

mcqs.q: If the angle of incidence on a plane mirror is 30°, the angle of reflection is:
mcqs.why: By the law of reflection ∠r = ∠i, so an angle of incidence of 30° gives an angle of reflection of 30°.

mcqs.q: A clear image is formed by which type of reflection?
mcqs.why: Regular reflection from a smooth, polished surface keeps the reflected rays parallel and forms a clear image; diffuse reflection from rough surfaces forms no image.

lessons.title: Refraction, Dispersion and the Rainbow
lessons.notes_html:
Refraction is the bending of light when it passes from one medium to another, due to the change in its speed.

Bending Rules

  • When light enters from a rarer medium to a denser medium, the refracted ray bends towards the normal (∠r < ∠i).
  • When light enters from a denser medium to a rarer medium, the refracted ray bends away from the normal (∠r > ∠i).
  • When light passes from one medium to another, its speed and wavelength change, but its frequency does not change.

Laws of refraction: (1) The incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal all lie in the same plane. (2) For two given media, the ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction is constant (Snell's law).

Dispersion and the Spectrum

The process of separation of light into colours is called dispersion. White light splits into a spectrum of seven colours, in order: Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange and Red (VIBGYOR). Violet is the most refracted colour and red is the least refracted. The primary colours of light are red, green and blue.

The Rainbow

A rainbow is formed when sunlight passes through raindrops in the air. The drops act like tiny prisms: the white light is refracted as it enters the drop, dispersed into its seven colours, reflected inside the drop and refracted again as it leaves it — reflection, refraction and dispersion together.

mcqs.q: When light enters from a rarer medium to a dense medium, the refracted ray will be:
mcqs.why: Going from a rarer to a denser medium, light slows down and the refracted ray bends towards the normal, so ∠r < ∠i.

mcqs.q: When light enters from a dense medium to a rarer medium, the relation between ∠i and ∠r is:
mcqs.why: Going from a denser to a rarer medium, light speeds up and bends away from the normal, so the angle of refraction is greater than the angle of incidence.

mcqs.q: Which parameter of light does NOT change when it passes from one medium to another?
mcqs.why: Refraction changes the speed and wavelength of light, but its frequency does not change — the colour of the light stays the same.

mcqs.q: The process of separation of light into colours is called:
mcqs.why: Dispersion is the separation of white light into its seven colours, as when it passes through a prism or a raindrop.

mcqs.q: The number of colours in a spectrum is:
mcqs.why: White light is made of seven colours — violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange and red (VIBGYOR).

mcqs.q: Which colour is the most refracted?
mcqs.why: Violet is the most refracted (bent the most) and red is the least refracted colour in the spectrum.

mcqs.q: Which colour is the least refracted?
mcqs.why: The fill-in-the-blank answer in the book: red is the least refracted colour; violet is the most refracted.

mcqs.q: A rainbow forms by the processes of:
mcqs.why: Raindrops act like tiny prisms: light is refracted entering the drop, dispersed into seven colours, reflected inside and refracted again leaving it.

mcqs.q: The primary colours of light are:
mcqs.why: The primary colours of light are red, green and blue; all other colours can be obtained by mixing these three in different proportions.

mcqs.q: The order of colours in the spectrum (from most to least refracted end) begins with:
mcqs.why: In order the spectrum colours are Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange and Red — remembered as VIBGYOR, with violet most refracted.

lessons.title: Spherical Mirrors and Optical Instruments
lessons.notes_html:
Parts of a Spherical Mirror

  • Centre of curvature (C) — the point at the centre of the hollow sphere of which the mirror forms a part.
  • Pole (P) — the point at the centre of the spherical mirror (the midpoint of its surface).
  • Principal axis — the straight line passing through the centre of curvature and the pole.
  • Principal focus (F) — the point on the principal axis where all the reflected rays meet (concave mirror) or appear to meet (convex mirror) after reflection.

Concave Mirror

A concave mirror is a converging mirror: its reflecting surface curves inwards and it converges parallel rays to its principal focus. It is used as a collector of light and heat. Images: object beyond C — real, inverted, smaller image between C and F; object at C — real, inverted, same-size image at C; object between C and F — real, inverted, larger image beyond C; object between F and the pole — virtual, erect, larger image behind the mirror.

Convex Mirror

A convex mirror is a diverging mirror: its reflecting surface bulges outwards. Whatever the position of the object, it always forms an image which is virtual, erect and smaller (diminished), formed between the focus and the pole behind the mirror.

Uses

  • Concave mirrors: reflectors in torches, headlights and search lights; dentists' and doctors' mirrors; shaving and make-up mirrors; solar cookers; telescopes.
  • Convex mirrors: rear-view (driving) mirrors in vehicles (wide field of view); safety mirrors at road turns and in shops; street lights.

Telescopes and Projector

A refractive telescope uses lenses; the distortion produced by lens-based telescopes is due to chromatic aberration. A reflective telescope uses a large concave (spherical) mirror to collect and focus light, so it is free of chromatic aberration and can be made much larger. A projector makes the given image brighter and projects it on a screen; the image is focused on the screen by a projector's lens system.

mcqs.q: Which spherical mirror is used as a collector of light and heat?
mcqs.why: A concave mirror converges parallel rays to its principal focus, so it is used as a collector of light and heat, e.g. in solar cookers.

mcqs.q: The image produced by a convex mirror is always:
mcqs.why: Whatever the position of the object, a convex mirror always forms a virtual, erect and smaller image between the focus and the pole behind the mirror.

mcqs.q: If the object is placed at the centre of curvature of a concave mirror, the image is:
options: Of the same size, real and inverted, at C
mcqs.why: For a concave mirror, an object at C gives a real, inverted image of the same size at C; beyond C the image is smaller, and between F and the pole it is virtual and larger.

mcqs.q: The pole of a spherical mirror is:
options: The centre of the hollow sphere
The midpoint of the mirror's surface
mcqs.why: The pole is the point at the centre of the spherical mirror (midpoint of its surface); the centre of curvature is the centre of the hollow sphere of which the mirror is a part.

mcqs.q: The principal axis is the line passing through:
options: The focus and the pole only
The centre of curvature and the pole
mcqs.why: The principal axis is a straight line passing through the centre of curvature (C) and the pole (P) of the mirror; the principal focus lies on it.

mcqs.q: Convex mirrors are used as rear-view mirrors in vehicles because they:
options: Give an erect image and a wide field of view
mcqs.why: A convex mirror always forms an erect, diminished image and gives a wide field of view, so drivers can see more traffic behind them.

mcqs.q: The distortion produced by lens-based (refractive) telescopes is due to:
mcqs.why: The fill-in-the-blank answer in the book: the distortion produced by lens-based telescopes is due to chromatic aberration; mirror telescopes avoid it.

mcqs.q: A reflective telescope collects and focuses light by using a:
mcqs.why: A reflecting telescope uses a large concave mirror as its main collector; the mirror reflects and converges light to a focus, free of chromatic aberration.

mcqs.q: In a projector, the given image is focused on a screen by:
mcqs.why: The fill-in answer in the book: the given image is focused on a screen by a projector, which makes the image brighter and projects a large, real, inverted image on the screen.

mcqs.q: A concave mirror is called a converging mirror because it:
options: Converges parallel rays to its principal focus after reflection
mcqs.why: The reflecting surface of a concave mirror curves inwards and converges sunlight (parallel rays) to its principal focus; a convex mirror diverges rays.

lessons.title: Force, Net Force and Balanced Forces
lessons.notes_html:
A force is a push or pull which produces motion in a resting body or brings a moving body to rest. Its actions are: it can move a resting body, stop a moving body, change the speed of a moving body, change the direction of motion, and change the shape or size of a body.

Measuring Force

Force is measured in newtons. The unit of weight is also the newton. By Newton's second law, force = mass × acceleration (F = m × a) — the product of the mass of a body and its acceleration is equal to force.

Net Force

The algebraic sum of all the forces acting on an object is called the net force.

  • If the net force is zero, the forces are balanced forces; they do not produce motion, e.g. a book placed on a table — its weight is balanced by the reaction of the table.
  • If the net force is not zero, the forces are unbalanced forces; an unbalanced force produces a change in motion — the object starts moving, stops, speeds up or changes direction.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an action of a force?
options: It can change the direction of motion of a body
It can change the mass of a body
mcqs.why: A force can move a resting body, stop a moving body, change its speed, change the direction of motion, and change the shape or size of a body.

mcqs.q: The unit of weight is the:
mcqs.why: Weight is a force (the pull of gravity on a mass), so its unit is the newton; gram and kilogram measure mass and pascal measures pressure.

mcqs.q: The net force of balanced forces is:
mcqs.why: When the net force of all the forces acting on an object is zero, the forces are balanced and they do not produce motion.

mcqs.q: Which force produces a motion in a body?
mcqs.why: An unbalanced force, whose net force is not zero, produces a change in motion; balanced forces cancel out.

mcqs.q: The product of the mass of a body and its acceleration is equal to:
mcqs.why: By Newton's second law, force = mass × acceleration; the fill-in-the-blank answer in the book is force (F = m × a).

mcqs.q: The unit of force is the:
mcqs.why: The fill-in-the-blank answer in the book: the unit of force is the newton (N).

mcqs.q: When a book is placed on the surface of a table, the forces acting on it are known as:
mcqs.why: The book's weight is balanced by the reaction of the table, so the net force is zero — these are balanced forces and the book does not move.

mcqs.q: The sum of all the forces acting on an object is called the:
mcqs.why: The algebraic sum of all the forces acting on an object is known as the net force; it decides whether the forces are balanced or unbalanced.

mcqs.q: The net force of unbalanced forces is:
mcqs.why: Unbalanced forces have a net force that is not zero, and this net force produces a change in the motion of the object.

mcqs.q: A mass of 4 kg accelerates at 5 m/s². Using F = m × a, the force is:
mcqs.why: F = m × a = 4 kg × 5 m/s² = 20 N. The product of mass and acceleration gives the force in newtons.

lessons.title: Density, Floating and Sinking
lessons.notes_html:
Density is the mass per unit volume of a substance:

Density = Mass / Volume

Its unit is kg/m3 (or g/cm3). A substance with greater density is heavier for the same volume.

Floating and Sinking

  • A body on the surface of a liquid floats when the density of the body is less than the density of the liquid. Its weight is then balanced by the upthrust of the liquid, so it stays on the surface, partly immersed.
  • An object sinks when its density is greater than the density of the liquid, because its weight is greater than the upthrust of the liquid on it, so it goes down to the bottom.

Advantages of Density

Density tells us whether a substance will float or sink in a liquid, helps in identifying and checking the purity of substances (e.g. milk and gold), and is used in designing ships and submarines, which float by keeping their average density less than that of water.

mcqs.q: Mass per unit volume is known as:
mcqs.why: Density is the mass per unit volume of a substance: Density = Mass / Volume, measured in kg/m3 or g/cm3.

mcqs.q: A body floats on the surface of a liquid only when:
options: The density of the body is equal to the density of the liquid
The density of the body is less than the density of the liquid
The density of the body is greater than the density of the liquid
Floating does not depend upon density
mcqs.why: A body floats when its density is less than the density of the liquid; its weight is balanced by the upthrust of the liquid.

mcqs.q: An object sinks in a liquid when:
options: Its density is less than the liquid's density
Its density is greater than the liquid's density
mcqs.why: An object sinks when its mass density is greater than the density of the liquid, because its weight is greater than the upthrust on it.

mcqs.q: The SI unit of density is:
mcqs.why: Density = Mass / Volume, so its unit is kilogram per cubic metre (kg/m3); g/cm3 is also used for smaller quantities.

mcqs.q: A substance has mass 200 g and volume 50 cm³. Its density is:
mcqs.why: Density = Mass / Volume = 200 g / 50 cm³ = 4 g/cm³. Dividing the mass by the volume gives the density.

mcqs.q: Density helps in checking the purity of substances such as:
mcqs.why: The book lists the advantages of density: it tells whether a substance will float or sink, and helps identify and check the purity of substances e.g. milk and gold.

mcqs.q: Ships and submarines are designed to float by keeping their average density:
mcqs.why: Ships and submarines float by keeping their average density less than that of water, so the upthrust balances their weight.

mcqs.q: When a body floats partly immersed, its weight is balanced by the:
mcqs.why: A floating body's weight is balanced by the upthrust of the liquid, so it stays on the surface, partly immersed.

mcqs.q: A block has volume 2 m³ and density 500 kg/m³. Its mass is:
mcqs.why: Mass = Density × Volume = 500 kg/m³ × 2 m³ = 1000 kg. Rearranging Density = Mass / Volume gives Mass = Density × Volume.

mcqs.q: If the mass density of an object is greater than the density of the liquid, the object on the surface of such liquid will:
mcqs.why: The fill-in-the-blank answer in the book is 'sink': greater density than the liquid means the weight exceeds the upthrust.

lessons.title: Pressure in Liquids, Gases and Air
lessons.notes_html:
Pressure is the force acting normally per unit area:

Pressure = Force / Area

Its unit is the Pascal (Pa): one Pascal is the pressure of a force of one newton acting on an area of one square metre — 1 Pa = 1 N/m2. The smaller the area, the greater the pressure of the same force.

Pressure in Liquids

In a liquid, pressure increases with depth, because the weight of the liquid above also presses down. Liquid pressure also depends on the density of the liquid and acts equally in all directions at the same depth.

Pressure in Gases

Pressure in a gas is produced due to the collisions of gas molecules with the walls of the container. When air is blown into a balloon, the number of air molecules inside increases; they collide with the inner walls in all directions, the pressure inside becomes greater than the atmospheric pressure outside, and the balloon expands until the elastic force of the rubber balances it.

Atmospheric Pressure

Atmospheric pressure exerts a force of about 100,000 N on one square metre at sea level. We are not crushed by it because the pressure of the fluids (blood and air) inside our body is equal to the atmospheric pressure outside, so the two balance each other. Effects of air pressure are seen in drinking through a straw, filling a syringe or dropper, suction cups and vacuum cleaners.

mcqs.q: Pascal is the unit of:
mcqs.why: The Pascal is the SI unit of pressure: 1 Pa = 1 N/m2, the pressure of one newton acting on one square metre.

mcqs.q: Pressure is defined as:
mcqs.why: Pressure = Force / Area — the force acting normally per unit area of a surface; force per unit area of an object is known as pressure.

mcqs.q: Pressure at the depth of a liquid is:
mcqs.why: Liquid pressure increases with depth because the weight of the liquid above also presses down; it also depends on the density of the liquid.

mcqs.q: Atmospheric pressure exerts a force on one square metre at sea level of about:
mcqs.why: The book's MCQ answer: atmospheric pressure exerts a force of about 100,000 N on one square metre at sea level.

mcqs.q: One Pascal is equal to:
mcqs.why: One Pascal is the pressure of a force of one newton acting on an area of one square metre: 1 Pa = 1 N/m2.

mcqs.q: Pressure in a gas is produced due to the collisions of:
mcqs.why: The fill-in-the-blank answer in the book: pressure is produced due to the collisions of gas molecules with the walls of the container.

mcqs.q: We are not crushed by the large atmospheric pressure because:
options: Air pressure is actually very small
