The pressure of fluids inside our body equals the atmospheric pressure outside
Our bones are made of metal
mcqs.why: The pressure of the fluids (blood and air) inside our body is equal to the atmospheric pressure outside, so the two balance each other.

mcqs.q: When air is blown into a balloon, the balloon expands because:
options: The rubber becomes thinner by itself
More molecules collide with the inner walls, raising the inside pressure above the outside pressure
mcqs.why: More air molecules inside collide with the balloon walls in all directions; the inside pressure exceeds the atmospheric pressure outside, so the balloon inflates.

mcqs.q: A force of 200 N acts on an area of 4 m². The pressure is:
mcqs.why: Pressure = Force / Area = 200 N / 4 m² = 50 Pa. Dividing the force by the area gives the pressure in pascals.

mcqs.q: For the same force, the pressure is greater when the area is:
mcqs.why: Pressure = Force / Area, so the smaller the area, the greater the pressure of the same force — that is why sharp knives cut easily.

lessons.title: The Hydraulic Elevator and the Rocket
lessons.notes_html:
Pascal's Law and the Hydraulic Elevator

A hydraulic elevator is a device used to lift a heavy load with a small force, e.g. lifting cars in workshops. It works on Pascal's law: the pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is transmitted equally in all directions.

It consists of two cylinders of small and large cross-sectional area, filled with a liquid and fitted with pistons:

  • The cylinder of small cross-sectional area is used for applying the small force (input).
  • The cylinder of large cross-sectional area is used for lifting the heavy load (output).

A small force on the small piston produces pressure in the liquid, and this same pressure acting on the large piston produces a large force — a small force produces a large pressure effect — which lifts the load.

The Rocket

A rocket is a spacecraft vehicle whose speed is higher than any other vehicle. It works on Newton's third law of motion (action and reaction). In a rocket, the hot gases are enclosed in the combustion chamber and, on burning of the fuel, are expelled backwards through a nozzle at very high speed (action); in reaction, the gases push the rocket forward. The speed of the rocket depends upon the speed of the hot gases thrown out and the mass of the rocket.

mcqs.q: The working principle of a hydraulic elevator is that:
options: A small force produces a small pressure
A large force produces a large pressure
A small force produces a large pressure effect
A large force produces a small pressure
mcqs.why: By Pascal's law the pressure from a small force on the small piston is transmitted through the liquid and acts on the large piston, producing a large force.

mcqs.q: Pascal's law states that the pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is:
mcqs.why: Pascal's law: pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is transmitted equally in all directions — the basis of the hydraulic elevator.

mcqs.q: In a hydraulic elevator, the cylinder of small cross-sectional area is used for:
mcqs.why: The fill-in-the-blank answer in the book: the small cylinder is used for applying the small force (input); the large cylinder lifts the heavy load (output).

mcqs.q: In a hydraulic elevator, the cylinder of large cross-sectional area is used for:
mcqs.why: The same pressure acting on the larger area of the output piston produces a much larger force, which lifts the heavy load.

mcqs.q: The function of a hydraulic elevator is to:
options: Lift a heavy load with a small force
mcqs.why: A hydraulic elevator is a device used to lift a heavy load with a small force, e.g. lifting cars in workshops and loads in buildings.

mcqs.q: A rocket works on Newton's:
mcqs.why: A rocket works on Newton's third law (action and reaction): hot gases are thrown out backwards and the reaction pushes the rocket forward.

mcqs.q: The speed of a rocket depends upon:
options: The speed of the hot gases thrown out
The pressure of the air only
mcqs.why: The fill-in-the-blank answer in the book: the speed of the rocket depends upon the speed of the hot gases thrown out (and the mass of the rocket).

mcqs.q: In a rocket, the hot gases are enclosed by the:
mcqs.why: The hot gases are enclosed in the combustion chamber and are expelled backwards through a nozzle at very high speed when the fuel burns.

mcqs.q: In a rocket, the action and reaction are:
options: Gases pushed forward; rocket pushed backward
Hot gases thrown out backwards (action); rocket pushed forward (reaction)
Both forces act on the gases only
mcqs.why: By Newton's third law, the escaping gases exert an equal and opposite reaction force which pushes the rocket forward.

mcqs.q: A hydraulic elevator is filled with a liquid rather than a gas mainly because the pressure in it must be:
options: Transmitted equally through the enclosed fluid to both pistons
mcqs.why: The elevator works on Pascal's law: pressure applied to the enclosed liquid is transmitted equally in all directions to the large piston, multiplying the force.

lessons.title: Conductors, Insulators and Electric Current
lessons.notes_html:
Conductors and Insulators

  • A conductor is a material which allows electric current to pass through it easily because it has free electrons, e.g. aluminium, copper, silver and gold (all metals).
  • An insulator is a material which does not allow current to pass through it because it has no free electrons, e.g. rubber, wood, plastic and glass.

Flow of Current

A conductor contains a large number of free electrons. When a potential difference (voltage) is applied across its ends, these free electrons start drifting in one direction, and this flow of charges is the electric current. A current in a conductor is possible because the conductor has free electrons.

Current and Its Unit

Electric current is the rate of flow of charges through a conductor: I = Q / t. Its unit is the ampere (A): the flow of charge of 1 coulomb in one second is called one ampere. Current is measured with an ammeter connected in series in the circuit. The work done on charges to flow in an electric circuit is known as voltage.

mcqs.q: Which one of the following is a conductor?
mcqs.why: Aluminium is a metal with free electrons, so it conducts current; wood, plastic and glass are insulators.

mcqs.q: Which one of the following is an insulator?
mcqs.why: Rubber has no free electrons and does not allow current to pass; gold, silver and copper are all metal conductors.

mcqs.q: The rate of flow of charge is called:
mcqs.why: Electric current is the rate of flow of charges through a conductor, I = Q / t, measured in amperes.

mcqs.q: A current in a conductor is possible because the conductor has:
mcqs.why: Metals contain a large number of free electrons which drift in one direction when a voltage is applied, forming the current.

mcqs.q: The unit of current is the:
mcqs.why: The fill-in-the-blank answer in the book: the unit of current is the ampere (A) — one coulomb of charge flowing in one second.

mcqs.q: A charge of 60 coulombs flows through a wire in 30 seconds. The current is:
mcqs.why: I = Q / t = 60 C / 30 s = 2 A. Current is the rate of flow of charge, so divide the charge by the time.

mcqs.q: Current in a circuit is measured with an ammeter connected:
mcqs.why: Current is measured with an ammeter connected in series in the circuit, so that the whole current passes through it.

mcqs.q: The work done on charges to flow in an electric circuit is known as:
mcqs.why: The book's MCQ answer: the work on charges to flow in an electric circuit is known as voltage (potential difference).

mcqs.q: Insulators do not allow current to pass because they have:
mcqs.why: An insulator has no free electrons to carry charge, e.g. rubber, wood, plastic and glass; conductors have free electrons.

mcqs.q: When a voltage is applied across a conductor, the free electrons:
options: Start drifting in one direction, forming the current
mcqs.why: The free electrons drift in one direction under the applied potential difference, and this flow of charges is the electric current.

lessons.title: Voltage, Resistance and Ohm's Law
lessons.notes_html:
Voltage

Voltage is another name for electric potential difference — the work done per unit charge in moving the charge between two points: V = W / Q, where V is voltage in volts, W is work in joules and Q is charge in coulombs. Work per unit charge is known as potential difference.

Resistance

Resistance is the opposition to the flow of charges (current) in a conductor. As the free electrons move through a conductor, they collide again and again with the atoms (ions) of the conductor; these collisions produce resistance, and electrical energy is changed into heat.

By Ohm's law, resistance is the ratio of voltage to current: R = V / I. Its unit is the ohm (Ω). Resistance increases with the length of the wire and decreases with its thickness.

Current and Resistance

Current is inversely proportional to resistance: I = V / R. If the resistance increases and the voltage stays the same, the current decreases; to maintain the current in the wire when resistance is increased, the voltage should be increased. From Ohm's law also, V = I × R.

mcqs.q: Ohm is the unit of:
mcqs.why: The ohm is the unit of resistance, R = V / I; current is measured in amperes, potential difference in volts and power in watts.

mcqs.q: The ratio of voltage to current is equal to:
mcqs.why: By Ohm's law, resistance is the ratio of voltage to current: R = V / I; the fill-in-the-blank answer in the book is resistance.

mcqs.q: By increasing resistance, to maintain the current in the wire, the voltage should be:
mcqs.why: Since I = V / R, a larger resistance reduces the current; to maintain the same current the voltage should be increased.

mcqs.q: Voltage is the work done per unit ______.
mcqs.why: Voltage (potential difference) is the work done per unit charge: V = W / Q, measured in volts.

mcqs.q: The unit of potential difference is the:
mcqs.why: Electric potential difference is also known as voltage, and its unit is the volt.

mcqs.q: Resistance in a conductor is produced by:
options: The collisions between the free electrons and the atoms of the conductor
mcqs.why: As free electrons move through a conductor they collide again and again with its atoms; these collisions oppose their flow and produce resistance.

mcqs.q: A voltage of 12 V drives a current of 3 A through a resistor. Its resistance is:
mcqs.why: R = V / I = 12 V / 3 A = 4 Ω. Resistance is the ratio of voltage to current by Ohm's law.

mcqs.q: A resistor of 5 Ω carries a current of 2 A. The voltage across it is:
mcqs.why: V = I × R = 2 A × 5 Ω = 10 V. From Ohm's law, voltage equals current multiplied by resistance.

mcqs.q: If the resistance in a circuit is doubled while the voltage stays the same, the current becomes:
mcqs.why: Current is inversely proportional to resistance (I = V / R); doubling R at the same V halves the current.

mcqs.q: Resistance of a wire increases with its ______ and decreases with its ______.
mcqs.why: Resistance increases with the length of the wire and decreases with its thickness, as stated in the book.

lessons.title: Electric Power and Safety Devices
lessons.notes_html:
Electric Power

Electric power is the rate of consumption of energy in an electric device: P = V × I (the product of voltage and current). Its unit is the watt (W); 1 watt = 1 volt × 1 ampere. Devices with less power, like an LED, consume less energy and have a smaller electricity bill than a heater, iron or hair dryer.

Safety Devices

  • Fuse — an electric safety device whose wire melts if the current exceeds its limit, breaking the circuit and protecting the wiring.
  • Circuit breaker — a safety device which automatically switches off (trips) when the current is too large. It is preferred over a fuse because it is fast and resets easily; a melted fuse wire must be replaced.
  • Earth wire — connects the metal frame of appliances to the ground (earth), so any leakage current flows safely into the earth and the user avoids an electric shock.

Overloading and Precautions

Overloading can be controlled by not connecting too many appliances to one circuit or socket, using wires of proper thickness, and fitting a fuse or circuit breaker. Our body contains water and salts, so it behaves like a conductor; that is why we wear rubber-soled shoes — rubber is an insulator and cuts off the path of current from the body to the earth. Other precautions: never touch wires with wet hands, use insulated tools, keep water away from electric fittings, and replace damaged wires at once.

mcqs.q: The rate of consumption of energy in a device is its:
mcqs.why: Electric power is the rate of consumption of energy in a device, P = V × I, measured in watts.

mcqs.q: Watt is the unit of:
mcqs.why: The fill-in-the-blank answer in the book: watt is the unit of electric power; 1 watt = 1 volt × 1 ampere.

mcqs.q: The product of voltage and current is equal to:
mcqs.why: The product of voltage and current is equal to electric power: P = V × I, as given in the book's fill-in-the-blanks.

mcqs.q: Which device has the smallest electricity bill?
mcqs.why: An LED consumes much less power than a heater, iron or hair dryer, so it has a smaller electricity bill.

mcqs.q: Name the device which melts if the current exceeds its limit:
mcqs.why: A fuse wire melts when the current exceeds its limit, breaking the circuit and protecting the wiring from damage.

mcqs.q: A device used to protect the circuit from a large flow of current is the:
mcqs.why: A circuit breaker automatically switches off (trips) when the current is too large, protecting the circuit; it is a safety device like the fuse.

mcqs.q: A circuit breaker is preferred over a fuse because it:
options: Needs a new wire each time
mcqs.why: A fuse wire melts and must be replaced, while a circuit breaker only trips and can be reset and used again at once — it is fast and resets easily.

mcqs.q: The earth wire is always connected to:
mcqs.why: The earth wire connects the metal frame of appliances to the ground, so leakage current flows safely into the earth.

mcqs.q: An appliance works at 220 V and takes a current of 0.5 A. Its power is:
mcqs.why: P = V × I = 220 V × 0.5 A = 110 W. Electric power is the product of voltage and current.

mcqs.q: We wear rubber-soled shoes when working with electricity because rubber:
options: Is an insulator and cuts off the path of current to the earth
mcqs.why: Rubber is an insulator; rubber-soled shoes cut off the path of current from the body to the earth, protecting the person from an electric shock.

lessons.title: Electromagnetism and Its Applications
lessons.notes_html:
Electromagnetism

Electromagnetism is the phenomenon in which a magnetic field is produced around a conductor when a current flows in it. It was discovered by Oersted. When a wire is wound in the form of a spring it is called a coil or solenoid. The magnetic field of a coil depends upon the number of turns, the current and the use of an iron core — all of these increase its strength.

Electromagnet and Iron Core

An electromagnet is a device based on electromagnetism: an iron core placed inside a coil is magnetized by the flow of current and becomes a magnet; it acts as a magnet only while the current flows, and the iron core greatly increases the strength of the magnetic field. An iron (soft iron) core is preferred over a steel core because soft iron magnetizes and demagnetizes easily and quickly when the current is switched on and off; steel keeps its magnetism permanently and is used for permanent magnets.

Applications

  • Door bell — works on the basis of electromagnetism: current in the coil makes the iron core an electromagnet, which attracts the iron strip; the hammer strikes the bell, and the circuit breaks and remakes repeatedly.
  • Loud speaker — its working principle is electromagnetism: the changing current flows in a coil in a magnetic field, and the coil and cone vibrate with the same frequency as the current — if the frequency of the applied current is 100 Hz, the frequency of the sound produced by the cone is also 100 Hz.
  • Electromagnetism is also applied in motors and generators.

mcqs.q: Who discovered electromagnetism?
mcqs.why: Electromagnetism — a magnetic field produced around a conductor when current flows in it — was discovered by Oersted.

mcqs.q: The magnetic field produced by a coil becomes stronger when:
options: The number of turns is increased
mcqs.why: The field of a coil depends on the number of turns, the current and the use of an iron core — increasing any of these makes the field stronger.

mcqs.q: An iron core placed inside a coil becomes an electromagnet when:
options: Current flows in the coil and magnetizes the core
mcqs.why: When current flows in the coil, the iron core is magnetized by the flow of current and becomes an electromagnet, greatly increasing the field strength.

mcqs.q: An iron (soft iron) core is preferred over a steel core because soft iron:
options: Magnetizes and demagnetizes easily and quickly
Is a better conductor of heat
mcqs.why: An electromagnet must switch on and off with the current; soft iron magnetizes and demagnetizes easily, while steel keeps its magnetism and suits permanent magnets.

mcqs.q: A door bell works on the basis of:
mcqs.why: The fill-in-the-blank answer in the book: a door bell works on the basis of electromagnetism — the coil's iron core attracts the iron strip and the hammer strikes the bell.

mcqs.q: If the frequency of the applied current is 100 Hz, the frequency of the sound produced by a loud speaker's cone is:
mcqs.why: The coil and cone of the loud speaker vibrate with the same frequency as the applied current, so a 100 Hz current produces 100 Hz sound.

mcqs.q: An electromagnet acts as a magnet:
options: Only while the current flows in the coil
mcqs.why: An electromagnet is an iron core magnetized by the flow of current in a coil; switch off the current and it loses its magnetism — unlike a permanent magnet.

mcqs.q: A wire wound in the form of a spring is called a:
mcqs.why: When a wire is wound in the form of a spring it is called a coil or solenoid; with an iron core inside it forms an electromagnet.

mcqs.q: Electromagnetism is the phenomenon in which:
options: A magnet produces an electric charge at rest
A magnetic field is produced around a conductor when current flows in it
mcqs.why: Electromagnetism is the production of a magnetic field around a current-carrying conductor, discovered by Oersted and applied in bells, speakers, motors and generators.

mcqs.q: Which of these devices works on electromagnetism, as named in the book?
mcqs.why: The door bell and the loud speaker both work on electromagnetism; the hydraulic elevator works on Pascal's law.

lessons.title: Casein Plastic from Milk
lessons.notes_html:
Plastics are polymers consisting of long chains of monomers (repeating units). Casein plastic is a plastic-like polymer made from milk: its repeating unit (monomer) is the casein protein of milk. When milk is combined with an acid like vinegar, a plastic-like polymer material is created. Vinegar (acetic acid) is the common household acid used to make casein plastic.

How It Forms

Milk contains the protein casein as small particles (micelles) spread in the liquid. On heating the milk and adding vinegar, the acid neutralizes the charges on the casein particles and makes the milk acidic, so the casein separates out as solid curds. These casein chains join and entangle with one another (polymerize) into long chains; when the curds are separated, kneaded and dried, they harden into casein plastic.

Procedure

  • Take a cup of milk and warm it (do not boil).
  • Add a few spoonfuls of vinegar and stir gently; white curds of casein separate.
  • Strain the mixture through a cloth and wash the curds with water.
  • Press and knead the curds into one mass and give it the required shape.
  • Leave it to dry for one to two days; it becomes hard casein plastic.

Items made from casein plastic: buttons, combs, beads, jewellery pieces and decorative items. Being made from milk, this bioplastic is biodegradable and environment-friendly, unlike synthetic plastics. Other kitchen acids such as lemon juice or orange juice (citric acid) can be tested in the same process.

mcqs.q: What type of material is created when milk is combined with an acid like vinegar?
mcqs.why: Adding vinegar to warm milk separates the casein protein, whose chains join into a plastic-like polymer — casein plastic.

mcqs.q: Which common household acid can be used to make casein plastic?
mcqs.why: Vinegar (acetic acid) is the household acid commonly added to warm milk to create casein plastic.

mcqs.q: The primary monomer (repeating unit) used in making casein plastic is:
mcqs.why: Casein plastic is a polymer whose repeating unit is the casein protein of milk; the long chains are made of casein joined together when acid is added.

mcqs.q: Plastics are polymers consisting of long chains of:
mcqs.why: The fill-in-the-blank answer in the book: plastics are polymers consisting of long chains of monomers.

mcqs.q: One item that can be made from casein plastic is:
mcqs.why: Buttons, combs, beads, jewellery pieces and decorative items can be made from casein plastic.

mcqs.q: In casein plastic formation, vinegar works by:
options: Making the milk acidic so the casein separates out as curds
mcqs.why: Vinegar (acetic acid) neutralizes the charges on the casein particles and makes the milk acidic, so the casein separates as solid curds which then polymerize.

mcqs.q: In the procedure, the milk should be:
mcqs.why: Procedure step 1: take a cup of milk and warm it (do not boil); then add vinegar and stir gently until white curds separate.

mcqs.q: After shaping, the casein mass is left to dry for:
mcqs.why: The kneaded curds are shaped and left to dry for one to two days, after which they become hard casein plastic.

mcqs.q: Which other kitchen acids could be tested in place of vinegar, as suggested in the book?
options: Lemon juice or orange juice (citric acid)
mcqs.why: The book's experiment design tests whether lemon juice or orange juice (citric acid) can replace vinegar, comparing the amount and hardness of plastic formed.

mcqs.q: Casein plastic is called an environment-friendly bioplastic because it is:
mcqs.why: Being made from milk protein, casein plastic is biodegradable and environment-friendly, unlike synthetic plastics made from petroleum.

lessons.title: Toothpaste, Soap and Detergents
lessons.notes_html:
Toothpaste

Bacteria in the mouth produce acids which attack the teeth and cause decay. The bases in toothpaste neutralize acids in the mouth and protect the teeth. To prepare toothpaste at home, mix baking soda, sodium chloride and calcium carbonate with water to create a smooth paste. Roles: baking soda (a mild base) neutralizes mouth acids and cleans; sodium chloride (common salt) is a mild antiseptic and cleaning agent; calcium carbonate is an abrasive which rubs away plaque and stains. In commercial toothpaste, sodium fluoride provides fluoride, which makes the enamel stronger and protects the teeth from acid attack and decay; toothpaste is a mixture of abrasives, fluoride, foaming agents and flavoring agents.

Soap Making: Saponification

The main chemical process in soap making is saponification: fats or oils are boiled with an alkali — sodium hydroxide (NaOH) — and they react to form soap and glycerol. Sodium hydroxide reacts with fats or oils to form soap; different oils give hardness, lather and mildness.

Detergents

Detergents are synthetic surfactants used for washing and cleaning various materials, surfaces and products. An essential component in the production of synthetic detergents is Sodium Lauryl Sulphate (SLS), the ingredient which acts as a surfactant. Detergents are made from sodium lauryl sulphate, soda ash and citric acid; they give powerful cleaning action and are effective in hard water, as they do not form scum like soap.

mcqs.q: Why are bases included in the formulation of toothpaste?
options: To neutralize acids in the mouth
To prevent the toothpaste from drying out
mcqs.why: Bacteria in the mouth produce acids that attack the teeth; the bases in toothpaste neutralize these acids and protect the teeth from decay.

mcqs.q: In soap making, what is the role of sodium hydroxide (NaOH)?
options: It reacts with fats or oils to form soap
It adds colour to the soap
mcqs.why: Sodium hydroxide is the alkali in saponification: it reacts with fats or oils to form soap and glycerol.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an essential component in the production of synthetic detergents?
mcqs.why: Sodium Lauryl Sulphate (SLS) is the essential surfactant ingredient in synthetic detergents, along with soda ash and citric acid.

mcqs.q: Saponification produces soap and:
mcqs.why: In saponification, fats or oils boiled with sodium hydroxide form soap and glycerol — glycerol is the useful by-product.

mcqs.q: The purpose of sodium fluoride in toothpaste is to:
options: Strengthen the enamel and protect teeth from decay
mcqs.why: Sodium fluoride provides fluoride, which makes the enamel of the teeth stronger and protects the teeth from acid attack and decay (cavities).

mcqs.q: To prepare toothpaste at home, baking soda, sodium chloride and calcium carbonate are mixed with ______ to create a smooth paste.
mcqs.why: The fill-in-the-blank answer in the book: mix baking soda, sodium chloride and calcium carbonate with water to create a smooth paste.

mcqs.q: In home-made toothpaste, calcium carbonate works as:
options: An abrasive which rubs away plaque and stains
mcqs.why: Calcium carbonate is an abrasive which rubs away plaque and stains; baking soda is the mild base and sodium chloride a mild antiseptic.

mcqs.q: Detergents are synthetic ______ used for washing and cleaning.
mcqs.why: The fill-in-the-blank answer in the book: detergents are synthetic surfactants used for washing and cleaning various materials and surfaces.

mcqs.q: Detergents are better than soap in hard water because they:
options: Do not form scum like soap
mcqs.why: Synthetic detergents give powerful cleaning action and are effective in hard water because they do not form scum like soap does.

mcqs.q: The main chemical process involved in soap making is called:
options: Neutralization of acids in the mouth
mcqs.why: Saponification is the reaction of fats or oils with an alkali (sodium hydroxide) to form soap and glycerol.

lessons.title: The Solar Cooker and the UPS
lessons.notes_html:
Concave Mirror Solar Cooker

A concave mirror is used as a collector of heat because it has a real principal focus. The rays of sunlight coming parallel to its principal axis are reflected and all meet at its real principal focus, which lies in front of the mirror at half the radius of curvature. In a solar cooker, the cooking pot (painted black) is placed at the focus, where the concentrated heat raises the temperature enough to cook the food; the cooker is turned from time to time to face the sun. A cooker receives heat from the sun through a concave mirror.

UPS — Uninterruptible Power Supply

A UPS is an electrical device used as an alternate source of electric power in case of failure of the main power supply. A UPS receives the electrical energy from the main power supply. Its network has four parts:

  • Rectifier — the section which converts AC into DC; the DC charges the battery.
  • Battery — stores the electrical energy as DC (a battery stores direct current, in chemical form).
  • Inverter — converts DC into AC when the main supply fails.
  • Static switch — an automatic switch which connects either the main supply wire or the UPS with the loads at a time; it shifts the load to the UPS instantly on failure and back on restoration.

In this way the load (computer, lights, fans) keeps working without interruption.

mcqs.q: A concave mirror is used as a collector of heat because it has a:
mcqs.why: A concave mirror converges parallel sunlight to a real principal focus in front of the mirror, concentrating light and heat at one point.

mcqs.q: Which optical device can provide heat to a cooker?
mcqs.why: A solar cooker receives heat from the sun through a concave mirror, which concentrates the sunlight at its focus where the pot is placed.

mcqs.q: The focus of a concave mirror is located:
options: In front of the mirror, at half the radius of curvature
mcqs.why: The principal focus of a concave mirror is a real focus in front of the mirror, at half the radius of curvature.

mcqs.q: UPS stands for:
mcqs.why: UPS stands for Uninterruptible Power Supply — an alternate source of electric power in case of failure of the main supply.

mcqs.q: The section in a UPS system which converts AC into DC is known as the:
mcqs.why: The rectifier converts the AC of the main supply into DC, which is used to charge the battery of the UPS.

mcqs.q: The function of the inverter in a UPS system is to convert:
mcqs.why: The fill-in-the-blank answer in the book: the inverter converts DC (from the battery) into AC for the load when the main supply fails.

mcqs.q: Which kind of current is stored by a battery?
mcqs.why: A battery stores direct current (DC) — electrical energy in chemical form, supplied as DC; the rectifier charges it and the inverter converts it back to AC.

mcqs.q: The function of the static switch in the UPS system is to:
options: Automatically connect either the main supply or the UPS with the loads
mcqs.why: A static switch is an automatic switch which connects either the main supply wire or the UPS with the loads at a time, transferring instantly on failure.

mcqs.q: A UPS receives the electrical energy from:
mcqs.why: The fill-in-the-blank answer in the book: a UPS receives the electrical energy from the main power supply and stores it in its battery as DC.

mcqs.q: In a solar cooker, the cooking pot is placed at the focus of the concave mirror because:
options: The concentrated sunlight raises the temperature there enough to cook the food
The focus is the largest area
mcqs.why: The concave mirror concentrates the sun's light and heat at its real principal focus; the black pot placed there absorbs the heat and cooks the food.

lessons.title: Wind Turbines and Generators
lessons.notes_html:
Generators

A device which converts kinetic energy into electrical energy is known as a generator.

Wind Turbine

A device which converts wind energy into electrical energy is known as a wind turbine. The moving wind turns its blades, the blades turn a generator, and the generator converts the kinetic energy into electrical energy.

Design and Working

  • Fix three light, aerofoil-shaped blades on a hub; the angle between every two blades is 120 degrees, so the wind pushes them evenly and the turbine rotates smoothly.
  • Mount the hub on a shaft connected to a small generator (dynamo), on a tall pole facing the wind, with a tail vane to keep it turned into the wind.
  • The blades catch the wind and rotate; their rotation turns the shaft of the generator.
  • The electricity produced can light lamps or be stored in a battery.

mcqs.q: A device which converts wind energy into electrical energy is known as a:
mcqs.why: A wind turbine converts wind energy into electrical energy: the wind turns its blades, which turn a generator.

mcqs.q: A device which converts kinetic energy into electrical energy is known as a:
mcqs.why: The fill-in-the-blank answer in the book: a generator converts kinetic energy into electrical energy.

mcqs.q: The angle between every two blades in a wind turbine is:
mcqs.why: A wind turbine usually has three blades, and the angle between every two blades is 120 degrees (360° ÷ 3 = 120°), so the wind pushes them evenly.

mcqs.q: A wind turbine usually has how many blades?
mcqs.why: The book states that a wind turbine usually has three blades set at 120 degrees to one another on the hub.

mcqs.q: The role of the blades in a wind turbine is to:
options: Catch the wind and rotate, turning the shaft of the generator
mcqs.why: The blades catch the wind and rotate; their rotation turns the shaft of the generator, which converts kinetic energy into electrical energy.

mcqs.q: In a wind turbine, the energy conversion is:
options: Wind energy → kinetic energy of blades → electrical energy
mcqs.why: The wind's energy turns the blades (kinetic energy), the blades turn the generator, and the generator produces electrical energy.

mcqs.why: In the design, the hub is mounted on a shaft connected to a small generator (dynamo), placed on a tall pole facing the wind.

options: Keep the turbine turned into the wind
mcqs.why: The whole unit is placed on a tall pole facing the wind, with a tail vane to keep it turned into the wind as the wind direction changes.

options: Used to light lamps or stored in a battery
mcqs.why: The wind turbine converts wind energy into electrical energy, which can light lamps or be stored in a battery for later use.

mcqs.q: Why are the blades of a wind turbine made aerofoil-shaped and light?
options: So the wind can turn them easily and smoothly
mcqs.why: Three light, aerofoil-shaped blades catch the wind efficiently and rotate smoothly, turning the generator shaft to produce electricity.

lessons.title: The Universe, Astronomy and the Light Year
lessons.notes_html:
The study of the universe is called astronomy. Our universe is about 13.8 billion years old. It began with the Big Bang, and since then it has been expanding.

The Light Year

A light year is the unit of distance used for the very large distances in the universe. It is equal to the distance which light covers in one year: 1 light year = 9.46 × 1012 km.

Galaxies and Telescopes

The number of known galaxies in the universe is about 2 trillion. The Hubble Space Telescope orbits the Earth above the atmosphere and gives very clear pictures of distant stars and galaxies; its objective lens (mirror) has a diameter of 2.4 m, and it can see far objects till about 13 billion years (light years) away.

Space Probes and GPS

A space probe is an unmanned spacecraft used to explore the universe and study the celestial bodies; probes travel far into space and send information and pictures back to Earth. The first probe launched to space was Sputnik 1 (1957); Voyager 1 is the farthest probe from Earth. GPS stands for Global Positioning System — a satellite-based system which tells the exact position of a person or vehicle on the Earth.

mcqs.q: The age of our universe is:
mcqs.why: Our universe is about 13.8 billion years old; it began with the Big Bang and has been expanding since then.

mcqs.q: A light year is the unit of:
mcqs.why: A light year is a unit of distance — the distance light covers in one year — used for the very large distances in the universe.

mcqs.q: The value of one light year is equal to:
mcqs.why: One light year = 9.46 × 10^12 km: light travels at 3 × 10^8 m/s for a whole year to cover this distance.

mcqs.q: The number of known galaxies in the universe is about:
mcqs.why: There are about 2 trillion known galaxies in the universe, each a group of millions or billions of stars held together by gravity.

mcqs.q: The universe began with the:

mcqs.why: The fill-in-the-blank answer in the book: Hubble can see far objects till 13 billion years away, because it orbits above the atmosphere.

mcqs.why: The Hubble Space Telescope's objective has a diameter of 2.4 m — metres, not kilometres.

mcqs.why: The first probe launched to space was Sputnik 1 (1957); Voyager 1 is the farthest probe from Earth.

lessons.title: Formation and Life of Stars: The Sun
lessons.notes_html:
Stars are self-luminous gaseous bodies — a star is the celestial body that gives out its own light, unlike the moon, planets and satellites.

Formation of a Star

A star is formed when a cold cloud of hydrogen, helium and tiny dust particles contracts under gravity over millions of years; as the cloud contracts, its density increases and the temperature of its core rises until nuclear fusion starts — a star is born.

The Main Sequence

The region in which a star lives after its formation is called the main sequence. A star spends most of its life there, steadily burning hydrogen into helium, and in this region its temperature and luminosity remain (almost) constant. Our Sun is a main sequence star, and a red dwarf is also a star in the main sequence.

The Sun

  • The Sun is the star situated at the centre of our solar system; it was formed about 4.6 billion years ago from clouds of hot gas.
  • It generates its energy by nuclear fusion in its core, converting its fuel hydrogen into helium.
  • The temperature of its outer surface is about 6000 °C and its diameter is about 1.4 million km.
  • Its total age (life span) is about 10 billion years, so it will keep shining for about 5 billion years more.
  • The nearest star to the Sun is Proxima Centauri.
  • The core is the central and hottest part of a star, where nuclear fusion takes place.

mcqs.q: Which one of the following celestial bodies is self-luminous?
mcqs.why: A star gives out its own light and heat by nuclear fusion; the moon, planets and satellites only reflect the light of a star.

mcqs.q: Which star is situated at the centre of our solar system?
mcqs.why: The Sun is the star at the centre of our solar system, formed about 4.6 billion years ago from clouds of hot gas.

mcqs.q: The fuel that the Sun uses to generate its energy is:
mcqs.why: The Sun generates energy by nuclear fusion in its core, converting hydrogen (its fuel) into helium and releasing huge energy.

mcqs.q: The temperature of the outer surface of the Sun is about:
mcqs.why: The book's MCQ answer: the temperature of the outer surface of the Sun is about 6000 °C; its core is far hotter, where fusion takes place.

mcqs.q: The region in which a star lives after its formation, where its temperature and luminosity remain constant, is called the:
mcqs.why: A star spends most of its life in the main sequence, steadily burning hydrogen into helium at an almost constant temperature and luminosity.

mcqs.q: The formation of a star takes about:
mcqs.why: A star is formed in millions of years as a cloud of hydrogen, helium and dust contracts slowly under gravity until fusion starts in its core.

lessons.title: Death of Stars: Dwarfs, Neutron Stars and Black Holes
lessons.notes_html:
End of a Star's Life

When a star's nuclear fuel is exhausted, its end depends on its mass. During its life a star's density changes: it may expand (density decreases — red giant) or collapse under its own gravity (density increases greatly).

  • Red dwarf — a star in the main sequence which is red due to its cool temperature; it is small and burns its fuel very slowly.
  • White dwarf — when the mass of a star becomes equal to or less than the mass of the Sun due to exhaustion of its nuclear fuel, the star collapses into a small, very dense and hot white body which slowly cools down; it finally becomes a black dwarf.
  • Neutron star — formed when the core of a massive star explodes and its electrons and protons combine to form neutrons. It is extremely dense (typical density about 1017 kg/m3). A pulsar is an example of a neutron star, and it has a strong magnetic field.
  • Black hole — an object whose gravity is so strong that nothing can escape from it, not even light, because its escape velocity is more than the speed of light. It has the strongest gravity.

Solar Mass

A solar mass is the unit of mass used for stars, equal to the mass of the Sun: 1 solar mass = 2 × 1030 kg. The masses of stars and galaxies are expressed in solar masses.

mcqs.q: A star in the main sequence which is red due to its cool temperature, small and slow-burning, is a:
mcqs.why: A red dwarf is a main sequence star which is red due to its cool temperature; it is small and burns its fuel very slowly.

mcqs.q: A white dwarf is formed when:
options: The mass of a star becomes equal to or less than the Sun's mass after its fuel is exhausted
mcqs.why: When the nuclear fuel is exhausted and the star's mass is equal to or less than the mass of the Sun, it collapses into a small, dense, hot white dwarf.

mcqs.q: The combination of electrons and protons forms a:
mcqs.why: When the core of a massive star explodes, its electrons and protons combine to form neutrons, producing a neutron star.

mcqs.q: An example of a neutron star is a:
mcqs.why: A pulsar is an example of a neutron star; it is extremely dense and has a strong magnetic field.

mcqs.q: Which one of the following has the strongest gravity?
mcqs.why: A black hole's gravity is so strong that nothing can escape from it, not even light, because its escape velocity exceeds the speed of light.

mcqs.q: Which star has an escape velocity more than the speed of light?
mcqs.why: Only a black hole has an escape velocity more than the speed of light, so even light cannot escape from it.

mcqs.q: The typical value of the density of a neutron star is about:
mcqs.why: A neutron star is extremely dense — about 10^17 kg/m³ — because a massive star's core has collapsed into neutrons.

mcqs.q: Which star has a strong magnetic field?
mcqs.why: The fill-in-the-blank answer in the book: a pulsar (a neutron star) has a strong magnetic field.

mcqs.q: The value of one solar mass is equal to:
mcqs.why: One solar mass is the mass of the Sun, about 2 × 10^30 kg; masses of stars and galaxies are expressed in solar masses.

mcqs.q: After cooling down completely, a white dwarf finally becomes a:
mcqs.why: A star of mass equal to or less than the Sun becomes a white dwarf at its death and finally cools into a black dwarf.

lessons.title: Galaxies and Their Types
lessons.notes_html:
A galaxy is a group of stars (millions or billions of stars) held together by gravity, along with gas and dust. Galaxies were formed from huge clouds of gas and dust in the early universe which contracted under gravity and broke into groups of stars. A cluster is a group of stars or galaxies whose members are close to one another — clusters are much larger structures made of many galaxies grouped together.

Types of Galaxies

  • Spiral galaxies — they have a central bulge and spiral arms, and contain both young and old stars. The Milky Way and Andromeda are spiral galaxies. Young stars are an example found in spiral galaxies.
  • Elliptical galaxies — oval or spherical in shape and mostly contain old stars. The largest are called giant elliptical galaxies (trillions of stars, very massive and luminous); the smallest are called dwarf elliptical galaxies (only millions of stars, small and faint).
  • Irregular galaxies — they have no regular shape and contain much gas, dust and young stars.

Our Milky Way

The Milky Way is a spiral galaxy — a dense band of dim stars — containing about 200 billion stars, with a diameter of about 100,000 light years. Our Sun is one of its stars.

mcqs.q: The Milky Way galaxy is an example of:
mcqs.why: The Milky Way is a spiral galaxy with a central bulge and spiral arms, containing about 200 billion stars.

mcqs.q: Which type of galaxy contains both young and old stars?
mcqs.why: Spiral galaxies contain both young and old stars; elliptical galaxies mostly contain old stars and irregular ones much gas, dust and young stars.

mcqs.q: A galaxy is:
options: A group of stars held together by gravity, along with gas and dust
A cloud of gas with no stars
mcqs.why: A galaxy is a group of millions or billions of stars held together by gravity, together with gas and dust; groups of galaxies form clusters.

mcqs.q: The number of stars present in the Milky Way galaxy is about:
mcqs.why: The fill-in-the-blank answer in the book: the Milky Way contains about 200 billion stars and has a diameter of about 100,000 light years.

mcqs.q: The diameter of the Milky Way galaxy is about:
mcqs.why: The Milky Way's diameter is about 100,000 light years; a light year is 9.46 × 10^12 km, so the galaxy is enormous.

mcqs.q: The largest elliptical galaxies are called:
mcqs.why: The largest elliptical galaxies are giant ellipticals, containing trillions of stars; the smallest are dwarf ellipticals with only millions of stars.

mcqs.q: The smallest elliptical galaxies are called:
mcqs.why: Dwarf elliptical galaxies are the smallest ellipticals — small and faint with only millions of stars, unlike the giant ellipticals.

mcqs.q: A cluster differs from a galaxy because a cluster is:
options: A much larger structure made of many galaxies (or stars) grouped together
mcqs.why: A galaxy is a group of stars held by gravity; a cluster is a group of galaxies (or stars) close to one another — a much larger structure.

mcqs.q: Irregular galaxies are those which:
options: Have no regular shape and contain much gas, dust and young stars
mcqs.why: Irregular galaxies have no regular shape and contain much gas, dust and young stars; spiral galaxies have arms and elliptical ones are oval.

mcqs.q: Young stars are an example of stars found in which galaxies?
mcqs.why: The fill-in-the-blank answer in the book: young stars are an example of spiral galaxies, which contain both young and old stars.
